AI-Golden Path Last updated on Oct 26, 2026 by SAP The SAP's AI Golden Path is the starting point for developing AI applications across the SAP ecosystem. It contains recommendations, best practices, and tutorials to help you understand the AI technology stack, identify suitable tools and services, and design, deliver, and extend enterprise-grade AI solutions on SAP technology. It serves as a central entry point into our approach for building AI-native applications, covering everything from data and AI foundation services to agentic architectures and Joule.
documents.s: SAP's AI Golden Path for Building Enterprise AI

documents.t: If you're an architect or AI project lead, this guide helps you to plan the architecture of your AI application and choose the right AI capabilities, data layers, and runtime services within the SAP ecosystem. If you're a developer, this guide helps you to select the appropriate tools, SDKs, and frameworks for building and integrating AI features. If you're a product manager, this guide helps you to understand the AI development lifecycle, available technologies, and best practices for delivering AI use cases.

Before starting your AI development journey, you may want to familiarize yourself with the following documents: SAP Business AI Platform Developer Guide Starting point for developing business applications on SAP Business AI Platform. It contains recommendations and best practices for development projects on SAP Business AI Platform.
Use this guide to navigate the AI development lifecycle, from understanding the available technology to implementing and scaling AI use cases.

The first step toward building an AI application is understanding the technology stack available within SAP. This includes: Agent Layer — including skills for the Agent Harness, content-based AI Agents built with Joule Studio, code-based AI Agents built with open-source frameworks and SAP's generative AI hub, Joule, and agent tools (MCP). AI Layer — powered by AI Core (including generative AI hub), and SAP HANA Cloud (including Vector Engine, Knowledge Graph Engine, PAL, SparkML), enabling model training, orchestration, and interaction through generative and agentic interfaces. Data Layer — powered by SAP HANA Cloud, Business Data Cloud, and partner technologies like Databricks and Snowflake for advanced analytics and data science. See Technology Decision Tree for details.

Choosing the correct AI approach depends on the use case and business problem: Agentic Workflows & AI Agents – Context-aware automation, orchestration, and dynamic decision-making. Generative AI & LLMs – Natural language, summarization, and conversational use cases. Classic Machine Learning (ML) on AI Core – Predictive analytics, optimization, classification. Relational Foundation Models – Structured data, tabular predictions. See Decide on an approach for detailed recommendations.

AI development follows a design-led, iterative process that ensures business value and technical feasibility. This guide structures recommendations across the key development phases: This guide mainly focuses on the Design, Deliver, and Run & Scale phases. Explore, Discover — Identify business challenges suitable for AI, evaluate feasibility, and define success metrics or evaluations (evals). Design — Create an AI architecture and decide between ML, LLM, or agentic approaches. Deliver — Set up the environment (SAP Business AI Platform, Joule, AI Core), develop and deploy AI applications, and integrate them into existing processes. Run & Scale — Run the application to provide business value. Evaluate & Improve — Measure accuracy, performance, and business outcomes; continuously enhance through structured evaluations. Extend — Build on top of existing applications or agents, integrating with partner ecosystems and third-party solutions. Get started with building in the Build and Deliver section.
AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP
documents.s: SAP AI-native North Star Reference Architecture

documents.t: As the enterprise software market enters a defining platform shift, one comparable in significance to the advent of the internet, agentic AI is fundamentally transforming enterprise software and business processes, reshaping how organizations operate, decide, and compete. SAP believes this shift will move enterprises from systems that execute to systems that reason, learn, and adapt, toward what we call the Autonomous Enterprise. This AI-Native North Star Architecture paper outlines SAP's target reference architecture and strategic vision for that future. It is not a detailed specification, product roadmap, or commitment to deliver specific capabilities, products, or timelines. Rather, it sets a strategic direction for SAP's AI-native, self-evolving enterprise platform, illustrating how AI agents, applications, business processes, data, context, and platform capabilities will increasingly converge in the next generation of enterprise systems. The document is introduced by forewords from Philipp Herzig, Anirban Majumdar, Stefan Nogly, Thomas Henzler, and Geoff Scott. These contributions reflect both SAP's strategic technology vision and the perspectives of leading SAP user groups, represented by DSAG and ASUG, highlighting a shared commitment between SAP and its customer community to shape the future of AI-native enterprise architecture. The paper is available on the SAP Architecture Center site and will evolve alongside the rapid pace of AI innovation, with quarterly updates planned to incorporate new insights, architectural decisions, and ecosystem developments. A downloadable PDF version is also available. Download PDF PVN Pavan KumarVice President, Office of the CTO, SAP Dr. Anirban MajumdarHead of the Office of the CTO, SAP

AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP The AI-native North Star architecture prepares SAP for quantum computing, where superposition and entanglement enable major acceleration in optimization, simulation, and machine learning. As we approach the early fault-tolerant quantum era over the coming months, preparing now helps ensure that SAP can adopt quantum capabilities once enterprise-grade hardware matures in the near future.

Quantum computing extends classical and AI-native systems by adding computational richness and depth for specialized problem classes. AI contributes cognitive reasoning, while quantum systems contribute amplitude- and phase-based computation, creating a continuum of intelligent and probabilistic processing that shapes the next phase of enterprise architecture. Architectural principles for quantum integration include: Quantum processing unit (QPU): QPUs operate as mathematical coprocessors that applications invoke for complex computational decision tasks and return classical outputs that flow back into deterministic workflows. Cloud-native integration: QPUs are accessed as secure cloud services through standardized APIs that abstract vendor differences and support scalable and interoperable consumption. Applications that use mathematical optimization can prepare today by using the SAP BTP service for mathematical optimization, which offers a path to quantum-enabled optimization. Scope for analytical and compute-only use: Quantum execution stays within planning, forecasting, and optimization because the no-cloning theorem prevents reliable replication of quantum states needed for transactional operations. Example: Quantum Machine Learning​ QPUs can be used for both training and inference. It starts with selecting the correct quantum model, which is trained on a QPU. The trained parameters are then stored classically on SAP BTP. For inference, the QML model with trained parameters is loaded in the form of a quantum circuit on the QPU and executed.
documents.s: How the AI-native North Star architecture integrates quantum computing

documents.t: By applying these principles, the AI-native North Star architecture establishes a hybrid model where classical determinism, AI-enhanced cognition, and quantum probability work together within a trusted enterprise foundation. This approach supports postquantum cryptography and prepares SAP for a secure and governed quantum-enabled future.
documents.s: The path forward: A quantum-ready enterprise

documents.t: AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP Each revolution in technology begins with a shift in imagination. The AI-native enterprise is that shift: a cybernetic system where software, data, and people continuously learn through feedback. It is not a feature but an architecture of intelligence where each interaction becomes a learning signal and intelligence compounds across the enterprise. This demands a new engineering paradigm: Context engineering to assemble the right information Harness engineering to ensure reliability and governance Specification engineering to define and improve behavior An AI Golden Path operationalizes this shift, guiding architects across deterministic and AI-native paradigms while enabling continuous evolution. What unifies these efforts is a single commitment: building systems that learn rather than dictate. A consistent lesson from decades of AI research is that capability emerges through search and scale, but search is only as effective as the space it explores. The system of context defines that space: structured, connected, and grounded in enterprise reality. In the agentic era, SAP customers hold a unique advantage that no model can replicate: decades of process knowledge, deeply integrated systems, governed data, and trusted decision frameworks. These compound into a new kind of enterprise intelligence that is reliable, transparent, sustainable, and deeply human. Technology leaders have built trillion-dollar platforms by compounding behavioral traces. The enterprise equivalent is now emerging: compounding context, decisions, and feedback loops. At SAP, this becomes the foundation of the Autonomous Enterprise, where systems that learn help ensure that each interaction strengthens intelligence and that outcomes, not features, define value. We encourage you to explore this shift, reflect on it, and share your perspectives as this vision continues to evolve.

AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP Customer-specific development services are AI-native offerings from SAP for customer-specific applications, reflecting the AI-native North Star architecture from SAP, where true value is created within each customer’s unique context. While standard SAP products are designed to scale across thousands of customers, these services address the enterprise reality that drives differentiated business value with customer-specific data, processes, constraints, and governance. They help maximize customer value and adoption of SAP software by delivering AI-native, customer-specific extensions that are living, upgrade-safe systems. These extensions continuously learn, adapt, and improve in production, providing true business transformation for customers. Customer-specific development services use AI-native, agentic engineering and accelerator-driven synthesis to start every engagement from a high baseline of completion, structurally reducing cost and time-to-value across the customer innovation lifecycle. They do this by unifying AI-native tooling, discovery, design, build, and hardening into a continuous, agent-orchestrated flow where solution assets evolve in real time and operational speed and efficiency are built in from day one. The AI-native North Star architecture is built to run on today’s infrastructure and absorb new computational paradigms as they mature.

AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP Trust makes collaboration possible. With identity, open protocols, and clear authorization boundaries in place, agents, data products, and tools can be registered, versioned, and shared across organizational boundaries. The SAP AI Agent Hub solution serves as an enterprise hub for discovering and managing agents, a marketplace where intelligent components are published, evaluated, and composed into solutions. The Agent Hub manages the full agent lifecycle: from planning and development through discovery and provisioning to observability, governance, and optimization. Agent mining discovers agents that already exist across the enterprise, giving organizations visibility into capabilities they may not know they have. Skills mapping connects agents to the organizational roles and business processes they serve, making sure the right agent reaches the right user. The ecosystem builds on three foundations. APIs and metadata, described through Open Resource Discovery (ORD), make each SAP capability discoverable and composable. Data products, governed through SAP Business Data Cloud, provide curated datasets that agents and applications can consume through standardized interfaces. SAP Knowledge Graph adds semantic grounding, enabling agents to reason across these resources rather than simply query them. Being callable is not the same as being usable by an agent. Interfaces need to explain what each operation does, what its inputs and outputs mean in business terms, and which permissions are required. APIs and tools organized around business tasks help agents choose the right action. These descriptions should cover customer extensions as well as SAP capabilities. On top of these foundations, developers, partners, and customers cocreate agents, models, and extensions that expand enterprise intelligence. Partners build domain-specific agents such as a logistics optimization agent, a regulatory compliance agent, and a demand forecasting agent and publish them to the marketplace with standardized metadata, quality metrics, and trust ratings. Customers extend agents built by SAP with their own business rules, custom data sources, and industry-specific knowledge. Each agent in the marketplace follows the same governance model: identity management, authorization boundaries, observability, audit trails, ethics, and sustainability. Whether an agent is built by SAP, a partner, or a customer, it operates under the same trust framework. Each agent's verification status is recorded in its metadata, and organizations can choose to block agents marked as unverified. The result is a network effect: more agents create more capabilities, more capabilities attract more builders, and the ecosystem compounds in value, mirroring the platform dynamics that defined the consumer era and now apply to enterprise intelligence.
documents.s: Ecosystem: The marketplace for agents, tools, and extensions

documents.t: AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP

For decades, enterprise software has been a system of record: it stores transactions and facts, enforces rules, and reports what happened. But these elements remain isolated and lack the context needed to explain why decisions were made, what alternatives were considered, or what worked and what didn’t. The reasoning behind enterprise decisions has remained locked in human judgment, scattered across systems, and lost between interactions. That is now changing. AI makes it possible to build a system of context blended with a system of record: an architecture where enterprise data, process knowledge, and decision history are connected across the enterprise landscape into a shared understanding, so that AI agents can reason over them. Agents participate in decisions as they happen, drawing on the full picture rather than fragments trapped in individual applications. Each correction refines the system. Each interaction adds to it. This learning evolves along three paths. Models advance continuously and supply general reasoning capability, a path broadly available across the industry. Enterprise context compounds and grounds that reasoning in business reality. And the system is designed to learn continually: what is established in one interaction can be retained as governed memory and drawn on in the next, within policy and tenant boundaries, without retraining a model. The system of context adds a compounding advantage that the system of record alone never had. The opportunity is massive. AI is on track to add trillions of dollars to global GDP over the coming decade with enterprise AI software expected to grow into hundreds of billions. AI-agent task duration is increasing rapidly: autonomous agents can already work unattended for hours on bounded tasks, and the trajectory points toward multi-day work within a few years. The trend is about duration, not scope. Agents will run longer on bounded tasks, while ambiguity, novel situations, and cross-domain reasoning will still require human judgment. The shift is redefining the value stack. Agentic experiences orchestrate outcomes across the enterprise, no longer confined to individual applications. Capabilities below this layer become increasingly commoditized and value shifts from software access to measurable outcomes. By 2028, pure seat-based pricing is expected to give way to outcome-based delivery. The implication is clear: in enterprise AI, context is the decisive advantage. Frontier models continue to grow more capable, but model capability alone is becoming commoditized, since every vendor can access the same leading models. What varies is the context over which those models reason. With the right context, software goes beyond predefined paths and reasons toward outcomes, application boundaries dissolve, and the enterprise learns. With five decades of business processes, domain knowledge, and industry expertise behind it, SAP has the deepest business context in enterprise software. Just as the harness around a model has become the deciding factor in what AI agents achieve, SAP’s business context structured in a knowledge graph and ontology, and the platform around it acts as a business harness: the same model, grounded in that context, delivers outcomes the model alone cannot. Research on systems that learn from experience has shown that they can discover strategies no human expert would have designed, and those strategies often become the winning move. Enterprise AI, grounded in SAP’s business context, operating across the full enterprise landscape, and acting on business intent, will uncover new paths to outcomes that no predefined playbook contains.

SAP’s deep business context creates a unique foundation for reimagining enterprise architecture for the AI-native era. In an AI-first world, an AI feature in an ERP system can summarize an invoice or suggest a journal entry. But it operates within the boundaries of a single application. It cannot see that the same supplier has open disputes in service management, delayed shipments in logistics, and a renegotiated contract in procurement. Three barriers keep AI-first confined. AI systems: Lack business and process context, leading to unreliable answers. Sit on disconnected systems without a shared data model, so they cannot coordinate across functions. Lack the governance to ensure accountability at scale. AI-native solves all three. Software operates across landscape boundaries as a system of context, creating a compounding loop where every interaction and correction helps improve future decisions. The delivery model evolves with it: from software as a service to outcome as a service. Intent-driven, agent-enabled execution learns and adapts continuously.

The Autonomous Enterprise is SAP’s vision for the future of how a business runs. It enables companies to respond more quickly, operate more intelligently, and perform better by design, using AI assistants and agents to manage and execute processes across domains in one connected, adaptive system. SAP delivers this through five reinforcing elements: The Joule solution as the new engagement layer, bringing together the right data, workflows, and agents across SAP software systems and beyond SAP Autonomous Suite reinventing how enterprises run, with AI assistants and agents executing work across finance, spend, supply chain management, human capital management, and customer experience Industry AI portfolio with built-in vertical process knowledge, data models, and regulatory logic SAP Business AI Platform unifying the SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) solution, SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP), Business Transformation Management solutions, and the AI Foundation solution to deliver business context, unified data, models, and enterprise-grade governance Accelerated adoption of the Autonomous Enterprise through the RISE with SAP journey and SAP GROW offerings, enabled by an agent-led toolchain These elements are realized through an AI-native architecture built on four reimagined layers: user experience, process, foundation, and platform. Together, they form the cognitive core: an enterprise intelligence system that integrates SAP’s business data, process knowledge, and reasoning models to enable enterprise systems to learn and adapt. Cross-cutting SAP-managed qualities help ensure that integration, identity, extensibility, provisioning, and observability are harmonized across the suite of SAP solutions. The architecture follows a shift-left and shift-down approach. Shift-left moves quality, security, and compliance checks into design and development, so issues are found and prevented before they reach production. Shift-down builds cross-cutting capabilities, such as resilience, security controls, compliance guardrails, performance, and sustainability, into the platform, so they are reusable and increasingly automatic by default, while each application team stays accountable for its application. Responsible and sustainable AI is embedded across each layer, generating ethical safeguards, transparency, and energy-efficient operations by design. This helps ensure that the shift to AI-native systems elevates trust, accountability, and long-term enterprise value while respecting planetary boundaries. This is not a replacement for what already works. SAP pairs two complementary paths: the deterministic path to safeguard trust, compliance, and governance and the AI-native path to evolve learning systems with data and compute. The distinction matters. Deterministic systems execute defined rules predictably, but they are rigid. AI adds adaptability, but without the right business context and controls it can produce wrong results or take inappropriate actions. The AI-native architecture closes that gap with three mechanisms. Context engineering provides the business data, domain knowledge, and policies relevant to each task. Guardrails constrain what the AI may do and validate what it produces against defined rules. Observability captures traces of decisions, actions, and outcomes, so behavior can be monitored, investigated, and improved. Systems of record remain the trusted foundation for enterprise data and transactions. AI adds adaptive reasoning, and controlled execution connects it to business outcomes. Together, they define the architecture for the AI-native era.
documents.s: Leading the next era of enterprise applications toward the Autonomous Enterprise

documents.t: AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP The foundation layer is where data and AI come together as the intelligent core of enterprise processes, giving every SAP customer a compounding advantage built on SAP’s five decades of business data, process knowledge, and domain expertise, structured in a knowledge graph and ontology. With the AI-first approach, data and intelligence remain largely separate: models run without business context, and data sits in silos without reasoning over it. The shift from AI-first to AI-native redefines how enterprise intelligence is built, grounded, and improved. In the AI-native model, orchestration, reasoning, and model services power the AI side. Governed data and semantic grounding, supported by SAP Business Data Cloud and SAP Knowledge Graph, provide context. Together, they store and compound enterprise knowledge that grows with each interaction. This enables intelligent systems to operate natively inside enterprise processes, with built-in guardrails for ethics, security, compliance, governance, and efficiency. The following capabilities define how this layer works: Orchestration: Joule orchestrates agents and tools to solve user requests, managing the lifecycle of agents however they are built, scheduling their actions, and aligning execution with workflow goals. Agent execution is coordinated across conversational, API-based, and event-driven triggers. This includes routing each request to the right agent, evaluating response quality, and resolving conflicts when multiple capabilities apply, helping ensure users get trusted answers and not just fast ones. For complex goals, Joule will decompose the task and delegate to domain-specific agents that execute in parallel and report results back for coordination. Agents are increasingly equipped with self-verification: internal feedback loops that check accuracy during execution, not just in post-hoc evaluation, reducing the error buildup that has been the primary obstacle to scaling multistep workflows. For work that spans sessions, agents will need to retain relevant context, recover from interruptions, and check progress against the original goal. Dividing work among several agents is useful when their contributions can be combined reliably and the benefit justifies the extra coordination. Model services: The specialized code base and domain knowledge of SAP represent a strategic advantage that general-purpose models cannot access. Frontier models lack native knowledge of SAP’s proprietary codebase, architecture patterns, and business logic. SAP-trained models combine continuous pretraining on internal code bases with fine-tuning and in-context learning, providing deep understanding of how procurement workflows connect to finance, how supply chain exceptions trigger approvals, and how your specific business rules work in production. The models are hosted through a Generative AI Hub. The Hub provides grounding services, to keep AI aligned with enterprise semantics, and optimization services (prompt optimization, test-time scaling, fit-for-purpose model selection), to improve efficiency and reduce inference overhead. Alongside SAP’s own models, the Generative AI Hub provides access to leading third-party models, including frontier large language models and open-source alternatives, giving customers the flexibility to choose the right model for each task without code changes. It is one hub with many models and consistent governance. This includes the SAP-RPT-1 AI model, built specifically for structured business data and trained on relational enterprise data, such as financial ledgers, transaction records, and supply chain tables, to deliver predictions without requiring customer-specific model training. Rather than having each team host models independently, this consolidation helps ensure consistent model lifecycle management, usage tracking, reduced environmental impacts, and capacity planning across SAP. Customers can use supported SAP-managed third-party models through the Generative AI Hub in SAP AI Core without procuring and licensing each model separately: SAP manages the commercial agreements, and customers pay for model consumption through SAP AI Core. Reusable intelligence: Core cognitive capabilities such as document understanding, tabular analysis, and visual inspection are implemented once and exposed as composable skills, helping ensure consistency and reduce duplication across applications and agents while minimizing redundant compute and infrastructure usage. Data and semantic grounding: SAP Business Data Cloud provides enterprise data, the SAP Knowledge Graph provides semantic grounding, and the Ontology layer helps augment the Knowledge Graph, unifying SAP and non-SAP data, thereby enabling agents with the trusted, context-rich, and efficient data and business context they need to reason, act, and learn. SAP Business Data Cloud helps connect data from across the enterprise into a single, governed landscape: cloud and on-premises solution systems from SAP, customer-managed legacy systems, third-party sources, and partner ecosystems. At its core are data products: curated, governed datasets with clear ownership, schema, authorization rules, and lifecycle management. Data products are the primary governed access layer for SAP data, enabling consistent and reusable consumption across analytics, data science platforms, and AI agents. Data products follow an authorization model and are accessible through multiple channels: SAP Analytics Cloud to create business dashboards and enhance planning, the SAP Datasphere solution for use in semantic data modeling, partner platforms such as those from Databricks Inc. and Snowflake Inc. for data science, and AI agents supported by Joule that access data through natural-language-to-SQL generation grounded in SAP Knowledge Graph. SAP Business Data Cloud will integrate tightly with the SAP AI Core foundation to train machine learning models and ground large language models, enabling the creation of new data products from the resulting insights. To help ensure agents have data access from day one, each customer's SAP application tenants come provisioned with an embedded data foundation that provides auto-generated data products. These data products are based on application metadata, removing the barrier of limited data product availability, so Joule and agents can query across application boundaries from day one. SAP Knowledge Graph is the semantic backbone of the AI-native architecture. It links natural language inputs to SAP’s structured metadata while reducing hallucinations, opening access to tens of thousands of APIs, data models, and business entities across SAP. When a user asks to “show me overdue orders,” SAP Knowledge Graph automatically discovers the right API, identifies the correct filter parameters, and constructs an accurate query, achieving accuracy that surpasses model-only approaches. SAP Knowledge Graph connects multiple layers of enterprise knowledge: API and service metadata: Definitions, endpoints, parameters, and relationships across SAP applications Business semantics: What “revenue” means, how “customer” relates to “order,” how processes connect across domains Data product metadata: Schema, lineage, freshness, and authorization rules for datasets Customer-specific extensions: Custom fields, custom APIs, and tenant-specific configurations layered on top of SAP’s base knowledge The long-term vision is a customer-specific knowledge graph with a shared enterprise ontology, where domain-specific knowledge graphs maintain autonomy while connecting via shared concepts, presenting a single logical view across the SAP solution landscape.
documents.s: Foundation Layer: AI, Data & Knowledge Graph

documents.t: SAP BDC Ontology Manager is a step toward that vision. It transforms data products into a context-rich, actionable business ontology - bridging the full enterprise data landscape and the decisions agents need to make. Rather than treating ontology as static metadata, it unifies SAP and non-SAP data into a single live knowledge layer: concepts, relationships, and policies spanning the entire data estate of a customer, from S/4 and LoB systems to other third-party sources integrated, unified, and enriched through Dremio and Reltio. This complete view is what makes the difference: agents deliver accurate outcomes because they carry the deep business context that only SAP can provide, grounded in decades of process knowledge no frontier model or SaaS player can replicate. Business Actions: Business actions, such as releasing a blocked invoice, are defined on ontology concepts together with their inputs, preconditions, and permitted roles. When an agent identifies a business object through the ontology, it also knows which governed actions it may take on it. Live Ontology: Continuously enriched by customer feedback, new data products, and evolving business processes, the ontology adapts to each customer's data landscape, becoming more precise and valuable over time while turning governed business context into executable intelligence. Context engineering and memory​ Every time an agent starts, it may have powerful reasoning capabilities, but it has no inherent awareness of the current task, prior interactions, or relevant business context. That context must be explicitly provided or retrieved. Context engineering solves this by assembling the right slice of enterprise information for each interaction while filtering out redundant, outdated, or unauthorized data, so agents can operate on context that is relevant and proportionate to the task while reducing unnecessary retrieval and energy-intensive inference calls. Joule and agents will share two forms of memory: semantic memory, which captures knowledge about the user, their preferences, and their working environment; and episodic memory, which retains summaries and goals from past conversations. Because the memory is shared, users can manage both forms in one place, and access can be limited to specific agents. Consider two customers with identical profiles: the same industry, tenure, and deal size. A system of record shows different discounts but not why. A system of context captures the exceptions, escalations, and precedents that shaped each decision, so the next agent facing a similar situation proposes the right action, not the average one. Over time, the system moves beyond responding to requests and begins anticipating the next business action. Agents persist context and reasoning artifacts across interactions, capturing decision lineage: what was known, what was considered, what was chosen, and what resulted. Each human correction becomes a structured decision trace. Together with SAP Knowledge Graph, these traces form a context graph: a living representation of enterprise knowledge that connects semantics, decision history, and operational context. Data was the moat of the last decade. Context is the moat of the next. Continuous Improvement​ Agent quality is maintained through structured evaluation cycles that span technical assessment of individual agents (goal completion, tool call efficiency), process and business evaluation KPIs, and financial and operational outcomes. This helps ensure agents are measured not just on technical performance but on business impact. As Goodhart’s Law warns: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” As an example, when an agent is given “resolve disputes faster” as its objective, speed becomes the target. The agent optimizes resolution time at the cost of customer retention. Evaluation is, therefore, a multiobjective optimization problem: rather than optimizing a single variable, the agent optimizes across multiple constraints such as resolution time, retention, and resolution quality. Business evaluation KPIs measure how each constraint shifts when the agent is involved, and those measurements become the feedback signal the agent uses to iteratively improve itself toward a stable optimum. As agents take on more complex work, the way they are evaluated will need to improve, too. Failures and human feedback can reveal gaps in the tests and help show whether a higher score also means a better business outcome. When the same approach works well across similar tasks, it could be captured as a reusable skill. The skill would be tested and reviewed before use, with references to the past interactions it was based on. Changes would be tracked so they could be reversed if needed. Over time, agents could propose improvements to their own instructions and skills, based on what evaluations and feedback show. This is a bounded, human-governed form of what research calls recursive self-improvement: people set the goals, permissions, and tests, and decide which proposed changes are adopted after the same testing and review as any other release. Workflows become cumulative assets that grow stronger with each cycle. The foundation layer builds the enterprise intelligence. Running it reliably, securely, responsibly, and at enterprise scale requires a platform purpose built for agents.

AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 26, 2026 by SAP This document compiles questions and answers from a series of interactions with SAP customers and partners, including multiple rounds with DSAG members, about the SAP AI Native North Star architecture. The questions range from clarifying concepts, planned capabilities, and the development roadmap to broader requirements and implications of the new approach. Some answers provide clear guidance. Others remain deliberately high-level, as the SAP AI Native North Star is a vision: it describes target concepts and architectural patterns for the future, and the fully defined end state is still evolving. Many of these concepts are already in development. Others are still being discussed and open. This is intentional. Moving towards an AI-native technology foundation is a broad and significant evolution that requires multiple sequential and parallel iterations. New concepts are developed incrementally and validated with early adopters throughout the process. See also the disclaimer down below.
documents.s: Frequently Asked Questions on the AI-native North Star

documents.t: Deterministic Execution Benefits Q: The advantage of deterministic applications and workflows compared with agent-based execution: they do not burn any tokens. A: This is correct. A key advantage of deterministic applications and workflows is that they do not require LLM inference for every execution step; therefore, they do not consume tokens. They provide predictable control flow, reliability, repeatability, and often lower cost for well-defined processes. The target architecture is not “agents everywhere.” Instead, it calls for a conscious decision and deliberate combination. SAP’s AI Golden Path provides guidance for deciding which approach, agentic AI, generative AI, classical ML, or relational foundation models, best fits a particular business problem and is applicable in general. A related presentation: “AI or not AI” AI Use Cases and Anti-Patterns (from the DSAG AI Topic Days 2026) LLM Cost Optimization Q: This concept triggers many actions that could be performed without an LLM. This could create substantial LLM load. What costs should be expected, and can LLMs handle this load at scale? A: LLMs will be involved where interpretation, reasoning, summarization, planning, or natural-language interaction creates value. This is not the case for deterministic operations that conventional application logic, rules, APIs, workflows, or queries can perform more efficiently and reliably. Cost, latency, scalability, quality, and risk must be assessed for each use case. Reuse and caching of intermediate results might become important optimization techniques. The generative AI hub provides optimization services such as prompt optimization, test-time scaling, and fit-for-purpose model selection. OpenTelemetry-based observability tracks model calls and resource consumption, so AI costs are visible per agent. Finally, our AI Golden Path offers guidance on which technologies to apply for which use cases or business process steps.

Joule Work Grounding Q: Joule Work: When changes are made to underlying software or table structures, what information must be provided to Joule Work? How does Joule Work obtain the required business context in such cases? A: Joule Work should be grounded in governed business context rather than relying only on the pure language model. The SAP Knowledge Graph is intended to be the semantic backbone for semantic metadata, business entities, relationships, and process knowledge. Persistent Space Memory Q: In Spaces, can a personalized contextual “DNA” be stored so that it is persistently available in the background for all interactions of the user? A: A memory functionality for spaces as a persistent, personalized context is planned across Joule and its agents, so it is not limited to a single Space. Joule and agents will share knowledge about the user, their preferences, and their working environment. Users will be able to manage this memory in one place, and access can be limited to specific agents. This user-specific memory must remain transparent, privacy-compliant, and under user control. Intent-Driven Process UI Q: How would an existing business process, such as incoming invoice processing, work in this UI concept? A: Initially, the Generative UI should not replace the business process with a single generic chat interaction. Instead, Joule Work is intended to let users express an intent, then assemble relevant information, agents, and tools around that goal. For an invoice-processing scenario, this could combine a “Space” for investigation and analysis, maybe discovering price or quantity mismatches, “Conversations” for questions and instructions, and “Jobs” for traceable, agent-supported routine work within defined guardrails. This might include finding documents, comparing invoices with purchase orders, identifying exceptions, analyzing discrepancies, recommending next actions, and routing cases for approval. The specific degree of automation remains a business-process and application-design decision. Shared Spaces Collaboration Q: Can generated Spaces be used by other users, or must every user create their own Spaces? A: This is a known and frequently requested capability. Spaces should support sharing of relevant artifacts and context where collaboration requires it. Still, sharing must respect authorization, ownership, privacy, and the separation of personal and team context. Cross-Application Spaces Q: Can Spaces also be created in SAP SuccessFactors? A: Joule Work is positioned as a cross-application workspace rather than an application-specific UI. In principle, it can surface authorized data, insights, and actions from SuccessFactors alongside capabilities from other SAP and non-SAP systems, provided that the required integrations, business capabilities, authorizations, and product support are available. It should not be assumed that every SuccessFactors scenario is automatically available in a Space; availability depends on the delivered and configured integrations. Enterprise Spaces Differentiation Q: Are Spaces essentially comparable to Anthropic artifacts with a DESIGN.md file behind them? What are the clear differences? A: There may be a conceptual similarity, both can present generated or context-specific work environments. However, the distinguishing objective of SAP Spaces is enterprise integration: they are intended to operate within a governed business environment and connect authenticated users, authorized data, business semantics, enterprise applications, tools, agents, and process actions. A Space is therefore not merely a generated interface or document. Unlike a free-form design file, Spaces are composed of a governed catalog of semantically described UI building blocks, constrained by layered design rules to stay on-brand, accessible, and consistent. Personalized Transparent Sharing Q: If the UI is highly personalized, how can results be shared transparently with colleagues? This seems to conflict with the idea of a single source of truth. A: Personalization and a single source of truth serve different purposes and can coexist. The single source of truth should remain the governed business data, metadata, calculations, process state of the underlying system of record. Personalization should affect how that trusted information is presented to an individual user. To share work transparently, Joule Work should make shareable artifacts explicit, and retain source data, calculation logic to make the outcomes reviewable, even when each person’s workspace might look different.

Agent Authorization Enforcement Q: Will LLMs adequately respect the authorization concept, or does the AI operate in a separate context with unrestricted access? A: The LLM (the component that underlies what is commonly referred to as "AI") itself cannot and will not be the authorization enforcement point. Access control will be enforced by the integration of agents and tools into the underlying system of record, which handles the necessary authorization checks. For agentic collaboration, the Agent Gateway is the central entry component which handles authentication, principal propagation, tenancy, and policy enforcement on agent level. The agent's permission can be configured as subset of the user's permissions. Agent Authorization Propagation Q: The established Joule principle is that user authorizations are inherited through PFCG. Does this principle remain unchanged for autonomously acting agents in Joule Work? Under which identity and with which scope of roles does an agent act when it executes proactively without a synchronous user context? A: For agents acting on behalf of a user, the user context and applicable authorizations are propagated and enforced. For autonomous agents that operate without a triggering user session, the agent can operate with an own identity, permissions, and audit trail. In either case, autonomy does not mean unrestricted access. The agent’s effective permissions must be explicitly defined and governed. The exact implementation, including how existing PFCG roles map into a specific deployment, depends on the application and identity architecture, but the principle remains that agent actions must be executed under controlled identity and authorization rules. User-Context and Authorization Propagation Q: Will Joule Studio support user-context propagation and authorization-aware access when an agent invokes a custom SAP BTP backend API through an MCP server? In particular, can the MCP-based API execute in the logged-on user’s context and return results according to that user’s authorizations? A: Yes. The user context is propagated so that the agent can access only the information and operations that the user would be allowed to access directly. In addition, agent permissions can be more restrictive than the user’s permissions. For example, even if a user is authorized to delete business data, the agent can be prevented from performing delete operations. This implements the principle of least privilege and supports governed agent execution.

Deterministic UI Coexistence Q: AI and Trust: From a business perspective, there is a need for a user interface alongside Joule Work that works entirely without AI. Business users must be able to verify what is stored in the underlying systems and ensure that information has not been distorted by AI. There are concerns that established SAP UI technologies, especially Fiori, may be deprioritized in favor of Joule Work. Consumer AI has produced many implausible or incorrect results. Regardless of whether the concern is objectively justified, enterprises fear that SAP AI could similarly create unreliable or hallucinated information, or that users could receive incorrect results because prompts were not precise enough. To build trust, a stable, deterministic UI is required alongside AI-driven interaction. If SAP advocates the coexistence of Fiori and Joule, this should be reflected clearly in the product strategy. A: This concern is valid. The AI-native Generative UI direction does not mean that deterministic, application-based user interfaces disappear. SAP business applications remain the systems of record, context and execution, while Joule Work provides an additional, intent-driven layer that can bring together data and insights. The architecture explicitly emphasizes reliability, compliance, transparency, user control, and privacy boundaries. For repeatable, transactional, regulated, or training-intensive tasks, stable application flows and established UI patterns remain important. AI should guide users to trusted application functions, explain relevant context, and automate only within defined guardrails. It should not replace deterministic backend functionalities. Fiori UI Roadmap Q: The coexistence of applications and Joule Work is perceived differently by DSAG members. Resources for application development, for example, Fiori, appear to have been significantly reduced with reference to Joule Work. Organizations now have several incomplete UI technologies, such as SAP GUI, Web Dynpro, and multiple Fiori versions, and are now being told that everything will become “Joule Work.” This does not match how representatives of business applications currently (have to) position themselves toward customers. A: See also Question. Joule Work should be understood as an experience and orchestration layer above applications, not as an automatic replacement for every existing application UI. The practical product roadmap and investment balance for each application area individually remain essential for customer confidence and adoption. The SAP Fiori design system remains part of SAP's AI Golden Path for application development, alongside CAP and ABAP Cloud. Deterministic Analytical Results Q: An analytical reporting capability based on the randomness of an LLM will never be accepted. Data must be definite and reliable. If two colleagues use the same prompt but receive different figures, the solution does not work. A: This is a core requirement. For figures, KPIs, balances, process status, and other facts that exist in enterprise systems or can be calculated deterministically, Joule Work should retrieve the authoritative values through governed data products and business services. The LLM may help interpret the question, explain the result, identify relevant dimensions, or formulate a narrative, but it should not invent or approximate system facts. The query itself is constructed with grounding in SAP Knowledge Graph, which discovers the right API or data product and filter parameters. Dynamic and Static UI Consistency Q: How consistent will dynamic UIs and Spaces be? How can new users be trained if everyone has an individual personalized UI? A: Dynamic UIs must remain consistent at the level of design language, interaction patterns, terminology, guardrails, and business controls. Spaces are more suitable for exploratory, goal-oriented, contextual work. For stable, high-frequency, standardized processes, especially those requiring formal training and stable UI, traditional application flows remain appropriate. For example, a dynamic Space could help a manager assess team availability and prepare a leave request. The formal creation and approval of the leave request might still use the existing deterministic capabilities.

External Chatbot Interoperability Q: Will it be possible to communicate with Joule from other chatbot environments, such as Microsoft Copilot? If so, will this provide an equivalent user experience? A: The target architecture supports agent interoperability through the A2A standard. External tools may access SAP capabilities through Joule agents, but they will not necessarily provide the complete Joule Work experience, including its workspace, context, governance, and orchestration. See also the Reference Architecture on Agentic AI & AI Agents

Document Processing and Grounding Q: Can I provide attachments in Joule Work, for example, to use an appropriate agent to extract data from a purchase-order PDF and automatically create a sales order? A: Document upload for document grounding is possible and can support question answering based on uploaded documents. A full end-to-end process, should not depend solely on free-form LLM generation. It should rather involve extraction, validation, matching against business data and an integrated and governed workflow. For this, the agent should use dedicated document-processing tools and APIs to apply business rules, authorization checks, master-data validation, and other controls before creating a business document in the system of record. Document understanding can also be provided as a reusable skill that agents can call.

Agent Gateway Availability Q: At present, agent-to-agent (A2A) communication is only supported in one direction (outbound)? When will SAP Agent Gateway become generally available? Source: Agentic AI & AI Agents A: SAP Agent Gateway is currently under development and is planned to become generally available around SAP TechEd 2026 time. Its purpose is to enable governed interoperability and collaboration between SAP and non-SAP agents through A2A communication. Agent Gateway and Cloud Connector Q: Is SAP Agent Gateway equivalent to a combination of SAP Destination service and SAP Cloud Connector? A: No. SAP Agent Gateway is a new component on the SAP Business AI Platform, designed for agent interoperability and governed A2A communication. It is not a replacement for SAP Destination service or SAP Cloud Connector, which address connectivity and secure access to systems and services including Cloud to on-prem systems. Role of A2A and MCP Q: Does SAP Agent Gateway also provide access to MCP endpoints in individual backend systems, or is it limited to A2A communication between agents? A: SAP Agent Gateway focuses on A2A communication and collaboration between SAP and non-SAP agents. Access to backend capabilities through Model Context Protocol (MCP) can be enabled through SAP Integration Suite, where MCP-based tools can expose SAP APIs in a governed manner. For more information, see A2A and MCP for AI Agent Interoperability Cloud Connector for on-Prem Access Q: If an agent running in the managed Joule runtime needs to access an on-premises SAP S/4HANA system, can SAP Cloud Connector still be used? A: Yes. SAP Cloud Connector continues to be available and is explicitly relevant for securely connecting services and workloads based on SAP Business AI Platform to on-premises systems. It remains an important connectivity option for agentic or AI-enabled solutions that need to invoke capabilities in an on-premises SAP S/4HANA landscape. See Pro-Code AI Agents on SAP Business AI Platform: Bring Your Own Agent Choice of LLM Models Q: Will users be able to choose or configure which LLM generates artifacts such as intent definitions, product requirements, specifications, or solution implementations? A: Agent builders can select the LLM according to their preferences or needs with respect to cost, efficiency and also sovereignty. See the Availability of Generative AI Models and more on Sovereignty Agent Technology Stack Q: What technology stack will be used to generate agentic solutions such as applications and workflows? Will established SAP technologies such as CAP, SAP Fiori, and SAP Build Process Automation continue to be used, or will workflows be replaced by n8n? A: The target is not a complete replacement of established SAP development and workflow technologies. Agentic solutions are intended to combine applications, workflows, integrations, skills, and agents according to the needs of the business process. At present, support or integration work is planned for technologies such as CAP, SAP Fiori, and React. n8n workflows are being considered for the relevant workflow scenarios. Architecturally, the important point is that applications and workflows remain part of the solution. Agent Traceability Q: How will the decisions, plans, reasoning steps, tool calls, and actions of AI agents be made transparent and auditable for end users, administrators, and auditors? A: The target is to log agentic activities so that execution is traceable. Actions triggered in backend systems should continue to be handled and logged through the normal controls and audit mechanisms of those backend systems. Agents will also persist context and reasoning artifacts across interactions as decision lineage: what information was known, what was considered, which option was chosen, and what outcome resulted. Human corrections are intended to become structured decision traces that contribute to a context graph combining semantics, decision history, and operational context. Agent Auditability Q: What about auditability, for example, with respect to audit-proof processing and compliance requirements? A: Agentic workflows need end-to-end traceability. The target architecture includes governance and observability capabilities, including OpenTelemetry-based traces, logs, and metrics, with agent identifiers and execution traces that connect each action to the agent, the work it performed, and the outcome. SAP Cloud ALM extends to AI-aware operations. Backend transactions should continue to be handled and logged by the relevant system of record. AI orchestration logs complement the existing application, security, and audit logs.

SAP-RPT Foundation Models Q: How about SAP-RPT-1? Is it a third-party frontier model that SAP has further trained? A: No, SAP-RPT-1, SAP-RPT-1.5 and higher are relational foundation models working on structured and tabular data. They are intended for the use cases regression, classification, and recommendation. SAP trains and provides these models as part of its AI capabilities for enterprise data scenarios. For details, refer to the SAP RPT-1 documentation. For a complete list of models, including LLMs and SAP-RPT, available through the Generative AI Hub, refer to the Availability of Generative AI Models. RPT Models Deployment and Productive Use Q: What role do SAP foundation models, especially SAP-RPT-1, play in the SAP AI Native North Star Architecture? Will they be consumable outside SAP AI Core or generative AI hub, and can customers self-host them? A: SAP-RPT-1 has a specific role as a model for structured, relational business data. It is trained on enterprise data such as financial ledgers, transaction records, and supply-chain tables, enabling predictions without requiring customer-specific model training. It complements the large language models and other machine-learning approaches. Self-hosting is not the intended productive deployment model. Although certain SAP-RPT models may be technically available through public channels such as Hugging Face, this is for experimental purpose only and not approved for productive customer use. For productive enterprise scenarios, customers should use the SAP-hosted and governed models available through SAP AI Core and the generative AI hub. See also the SAP-RPT Playground SAP-RPT In-Context Learning Q: For in-context learning in SAP-RPT, does the context data need to include all relevant target values? Otherwise, how can the model know the correct value? A: For a prediction or classification scenario, the context data defines the set of possible output values, the model cannot “invent” values. For regression, the target is a continuous numeric range, predicted values are calculated by regression and do not need to be exactly present as part of the context data.

Knowledge Graph Governance Q: Can customers inspect and, where appropriate, correct the content of the SAP Knowledge Graph? How are conflicting or contradictory facts resolved, for example, where SAP-delivered metadata and customer-specific extensions describe the same business concept differently? A: The SAP AI Native North Star architecture describes SAP Knowledge Graph as the semantic backbone that connects API and service metadata, business semantics, data-product metadata, and customer-specific extensions such as custom fields, custom APIs, and tenant-specific configuration. The long-term target is a customer-specific knowledge graph built on a shared enterprise ontology. Domain-specific knowledge graphs should retain autonomy while being connected through shared concepts, creating one logical view across the SAP landscape. This implies a need for governed maintenance, provenance, ownership, and conflict-resolution mechanisms for customer-specific content. The SAP BDC Ontology Manager (SAP AI Native North Star 2026 Q4) adds a live ontology on top of SAP Knowledge Graph. It unifies SAP and non-SAP data and is continuously enriched by customer feedback, new data products, and evolving business processes. However, the details are not yet defined for the user interface, governance workflow, or conflict-resolution algorithm through which customers will inspect, amend, approve, or reconcile contradictory graph content. Knowledge Graph and Authorizations Q: SAP Knowledge Graph includes authorization rules as data-product metadata. Are these rules descriptive only, or are they actively enforced during semantic traversal across entity and system boundaries? For example, if an agent moves from an S/4HANA supplier entity to an Ariba supplier entity, is authorization enforced at every source-system hop or according to the data product’s authorization model? A: SAP Knowledge Graph provides semantic relationships and grounding; it does not enforce authorization decisions. Data-product access is governed through Authorization Management Service, and access checks apply when the consumer requests concrete objects or data. In other words, the graph can help an agent discover that an S/4HANA supplier concept relates to an Ariba supplier concept, but it will not bypass the authorization checks of the relevant data product, API, or underlying access service. Knowledge Graph and LeanIX Processes Q: Will process knowledge from SAP LeanIX be incorporated into SAP Knowledge Graph? A: Process knowledge from SAP Signavio and landscape and architecture data from SAP LeanIX is expected to contribute to SAP Knowledge Graph, but this integration is still work in progress. Conceptually, the process and architecture knowledge will enrich the graph’s cross-domain business semantics and relationships among applications, processes, APIs, and enterprise entities. Custom Agent Access to KG Q: Will customer-developed agents be able to access SAP Knowledge Graph directly? A: This is under discussion. The current working assumption is that agents running in the SAP context, especially Joule and Joule agents, will use SAP Knowledge Graph directly for grounding when accessing APIs and data products and other business entities. For custom or external agents, the available integration model, direct graph-access APIs, authorization model, and contractual boundaries still need to be confirmed. Knowledge Graph Visibility Q: How will SAP Knowledge Graph be made available to existing customer-managed LLM platforms, agentic platforms, and AI assistants, not only Joule? Where will the graph reside, and how can SAP-managed and customer-managed agents share or combine context to create a unified enterprise view? A: The initial focus is on Joule and Joule agents using SAP Knowledge Graph within the SAP environment. The SAP Knowledge Graph will be the semantic backbone that grounds natural-language requests in SAP APIs, data models, business entities, and data products. For external agents, the currently described direction is indirect use through agent-to-agent (A2A) interaction, rather than unrestricted direct access to the SAP Knowledge Graph. This can allow an external agent to delegate an SAP-specific task to a SAP-side agent that uses SAP Knowledge Graph and governed data products internally. The long-term architectural vision is a customer-specific knowledge graph connected through a shared enterprise ontology, in which domain-specific graphs remain autonomous but interoperate through shared concepts. That direction shall support a more unified context across SAP and customer-managed domains.

Custom Data Products Q: How can a customer expose data from a custom SAP Business AI Platform application, for example, one built with CAP and SAP HANA Cloud, as a governed data product in SAP Business Data Cloud? What is the supported path for creating, publishing, and consuming it? A: SAP’s BDC recognizes customer-defined data products alongside SAP-managed and partner-defined data products. In the target architecture, a data product is a curated, business-ready dataset with meaningful metadata, including ownership, schema, authorization rules, lineage, freshness, and lifecycle management. It is intended to be discoverable and consumable by analytics, data-science platforms, and AI agents. See also Implement and Extend SAP-managed Domain Content in SAP BDC For custom data sources, the currently documented route is to integrate and model the data in SAP Datasphere, using its native connectivity and customer-managed storage and modeling capabilities. See also SAP’s BDC FAQ A Data Product Creation Agent is work in progress. BDC for Custom Development Q: Can SAP Business Data Cloud, particularly SAP Datasphere and SAP Analytics Cloud, also be used as a development platform for custom applications and custom analytics where no standard SAP solution exists? A: Yes, SAP Datasphere and SAP Analytics Cloud can be used for customer-specific data integration, semantic modeling, analytics, planning, and custom analytical content. BDC is intended to combine governed SAP and non-SAP data with analytics, planning, data engineering, and AI/ML capabilities. SAP also positions the broader SAP Business AI platform as the environment for building and operating AI-enabled solutions. Data Product Authorizations Q: When sensitive S/4HANA cost-center, ledger, or other business data is published as a governed data product in SAP Business Data Cloud, does the original transactional authorization model travel with the data product? A: A data product has its own defined authorization rules and governed consumption model. Its access controls can be deliberately different from the authorization model of the originating transactional application, provided this is designed and governed appropriately. A practical implication is that restricting direct access to source-system raw data does not automatically guarantee the same restriction in the data product. The data product’s own authorization design, including who can access which records, attributes, and derived metrics, must be defined, tested, and governed. Illustration: A user might not be allowed to display individual S/4HANA journal entries in the transactional system, while the user may be allowed to consume an aggregated finance data product in SAC. That can be appropriate, but only if the data product’s authorization policy intentionally permits the aggregate while protecting disallowed record-level detail. Authorization and Result Completeness Q: On Data Products: When users query a data product, how can they know whether the returned result set is complete? Are records excluded due to authorization reported separately, for example, as a count of suppressed records? A: Yes, the expected behavior is analogous to conventional authorization-controlled reporting: users receive only the records they are authorized to access, while unauthorized records are not returned. Unauthorized information is filtered out before it reaches an agent or other consumer. Read-Write Interface Choice Q: For an agent that must perform write operations, when should it use BDC data products and when is an MCP server or application API the better approach? A: Use governed BDC data products primarily for read-oriented, analytical, and cross-domain scenarios, such as aggregations, statistics, planning, trend analysis, or questions that combine data across lines of business. Data products are the curated and governed interfaces for dashboards, data science, and Joule-supported AI agents. For transactional or write scenarios, application APIs exposed through an MCP server are usually the better fit. Customer-specific MCP servers can be enabled on the basis of public APIs and made available to SAP-side agents. A write action should be processed by the owning application through its established write API, validation logic, business rules, and authorization checks. See also SAP API Policy

Central Agent Management Q: How can an enterprise manage custom agents centrally? Will there be a consolidated view of agents, their dependencies and access rights, as well as monitoring capabilities? A: SAP AI Agent Hub is the place for managing and governing custom agents centrally. It manages the full agent lifecycle, from planning and development through discovery and provisioning to observability, governance, and optimization. Agent mining discovers agents that already exist across the enterprise, and skills mapping connects agents to the roles and business processes they serve. The intended operating model also includes lifecycle management of agentic solutions and their dependencies. The Process Layer describes a solution as more than one isolated agent: it can include applications, workflows, one or more agents, APIs, and related dependencies, managed together as a deployable solution with a shared lifecycle. For runtime observability, OpenTelemetry-based monitoring of agents and applications, including operational health, agent actions, reasoning context, and invoked services will be used. Agent Deployment Q: How are agents deployed? Are they automatically deployed to SAP BTP or the SAP Business AI Platform? A: The expected deployment model is deployment to an automatically provisioned SAP Business AI Platform environment and its unified agent runtime. Both creation paths, pro-code development with an agent SDK and prompt-driven development through Joule Studio, produce the same canonical, code-based artifact and deploy to the same runtime. This supports portability, version control, auditability, and a consistent operational model. The differentiation between the platforms in this question is referring to a transition time when customers may have both in place. Agent Lifecycle Management Q: How will lifecycle management work for agentic solutions? If a change is required, how will the solution be modified, tested, versioned, and redeployed? A: The objective is to manage agents together with their dependencies, such as APIs, backend services, integrations, skills, applications, and workflows, and to control initial deployment and redeployment accordingly. Details are work in progress. SAP AI Agent Hub will play a significant role here. Sovereign Cloud Deployment Q: The infrastructure layer relies on hyperscale cloud providers. How does the architecture address customers’ sovereignty requirements, for example, where workloads must not run on non-sovereign public-cloud infrastructure or need to remain within a specific jurisdiction? A: SAP’s multitier cloud deployment model includes public cloud, private cloud, SAP Sovereign Cloud offerings, and SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site offerings for customer-selected or customer-owned data centers. These options are intended to support control over data, infrastructure, compliance, and the use of compliant large language models in line with local legal and regulatory requirements. Work on sovereign cloud capabilities involves SAP, hyperscalers, and other service providers and is in progress. See also the section on Sovereignty Agent Extensibility Model Q: How can customers extend or adapt SAP-delivered agents? In particular, will there be an approach comparable to traditional customer-specific enhancements, but without directly modifying SAP-delivered code? A: An extensibility approach is being designed and developed. Customers and partners customize agents without modifying the underlying code through four patterns: tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), skills as reusable building blocks, pre- and post-execution hooks, and instructions that precondition the agent's behavior with domain knowledge and operating guidelines. Further details will evolve in upcoming iterations and through early-adopter feedback. Services and Connectivity in Managed Runtime Q: What connectivity model will enable CAP applications running in the managed runtime to access other CAP-based services in the managed runtime? More specifically, can declarative deployment and service configuration, for example, through assets.yaml, be used to connect a CAP service to managed-runtime services, beyond simply exposing agent-to-agent connectivity? A: This is a valid requirement and is technically feasible in principle. The exact connectivity model, supported configuration, and timeline for general availability are still being clarified. Agent On-Premises Integration Q: Can Joule Work also interact with on-premises systems? Technically, this should be possible as long as an API is available. A: In principle, on-premises integration is feasible. The SAP Integration Suite and its MCP Gateway are the mechanisms for governed exposure of SAP and non-SAP APIs, while customer-managed SAP Business AI Platform environments can host integrations and self-managed agents.
