AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP Autonomous agents operate within enterprise-grade boundaries for governance, identity, and interoperability. Integration remains the biggest challenge in enterprise AI, and governance and compliance are not yet fully solved across industries. SAP is focusing on building architectural foundations that make these challenges tractable.

AI enables integration: Agents dynamically determine intent, select the right APIs, and orchestrate calls across systems. They learn from usage to improve quality over time, and they reduce environmental impact by removing redundant integration logic and minimizing avoidable system-to-system data transfers. Integration enables AI: Existing APIs, events, and data across SAP and third-party software systems become tools that agents can discover and use through open standards, without requiring new development artifacts. Two open protocols make this possible. The Model Context Protocol provides tool integration, enabling agents to discover and invoke capabilities across systems. The Agent2Agent protocol supports multiagent coordination, enabling agents built by different teams, partners, and customers to collaborate within governed boundaries. SAP participates in the open standards ecosystem to ensure agents interoperate across the enterprise landscape, not just within SAP. Thus, integration shifts from connector-driven to intelligence-driven.

SAP's strategy is to deliver a pre-integrated, AI-native Autonomous Suite in which applications, AI agents, and assistants operate as a cohesive solution. SAP-managed provisioning, functional and technical integration, and lifecycle management enable agents to execute end-to-end business processes across applications, accelerating customer time to value and differentiating SAP from point-solution providers. Preconfigured integrations and shared business context enable agents to coordinate actions across the suite, while centralized governance, observability, automated safeguards, and SAP-managed operations support reliable, secure, and accountable execution. This reduces customer complexity and allows enterprises to focus on business outcomes rather than assembling and operating the underlying technology. Agent traffic flows through a governed gateway that acts as the trusted bridge between agents, tools, and backend systems. It ensures that agents operate within defined boundaries and are only accessible when explicitly authorized for collaboration - whether across systems, applications, or organizational domains. The gateway handles the platform-level concerns that every agent integration needs: security, access control, identity, and observability. It provides a unified catalog of available tools, enforces who can use what, and routes decisions that require human approval before proceeding. Backend systems are always accessed through official, governed APIs.

Agentic AI introduces new categories of risk that traditional security frameworks were not designed to address. Agents make autonomous decisions, access external tools, and operate across trust boundaries. Multiagent systems acting across organizations magnify these risks. Regulatory frameworks, including the EU AI Act and US AI Action Plan, make AI security mandatory. Trust is what converts capability into permission to act. Without it, agents can advise but cannot operate. With it, agents execute across real workflows, accumulate institutional judgment, and become more valuable with each interaction. In the AI-native model, agents are first-class principals: they authenticate, receive authorizations, and are governed like any other enterprise actor. Each agent carries its own identity that combines an application registration, policy assignments for persistent roles, and scoped authorizations. Users can grant agents a bounded subset of their permissions for unattended execution to make sure agents never act beyond their authorized scope. Alternatively, an agent can act in its own right, with scoped authorizations assigned specifically to it. When a system-triggered agent needs to act in a user's context, it requests this through a task in that user's inbox and continues with the user's permissions once the task is completed. Third-party agents must also authenticate via identity services from SAP; agents without valid credentials are denied access. When agents from SAP call into third-party systems, the platform performs token exchanges on their behalf to maintain governed access across trust boundaries. The three-tier AI defense architecture from SAP addresses agentic threats through a progressive approach: Foundation tier: Zero-trust authentication, traffic inspection, prompt-injection detection, behavioral analytics, and cryptographically verifiable agent credentials. Entities are validated, and actions are recorded. Supervision tier: Deterministic control agents that monitor, sanitize, and authorize other AI agents. These supervisory agents enforce input validation, output filtering, and anomaly detection - with human oversight for high-risk decisions. Automation tier: Specialized AI agents that scale security operations through continuous audits, risk assessment, and policy enforcement. Identity management agents handle provisioning and contextual authorization. This layer embeds secure development practices into AI-assisted workflows, helping ensure AI-generated code is validated and compliant before release. AI is also an ally: intelligent agents audit systems, perform authorization checks, detect vulnerabilities, and enforce compliance early in development. This embeds a shift-left approach that prevents risks rather than reacting to them.

As AI becomes embedded across the architecture, shaping how systems reason, act, and interact, AI ethics becomes a foundational cross-cutting concern across each layer. It works to ensure AI systems are designed, developed, deployed, used, and commercialized in line with defined standards of trust and responsibility. Agents introduce a distinct ethical risk profile because they can not only generate outputs but also plan, act, invoke tools, and operate across system and organizational boundaries with limited human intervention. Their autonomy, scale, and ability to affect real workflows increase the potential for unintended harm, unfair outcomes, opaque decision-making, and weakened accountability. SAP helps operationalize AI ethics through a global policy framework, structured use-case review, defined oversight structure, and lifecycle controls integrated with security, data protection, risk management, and compliance. SAP’s approach is anchored in the SAP Global AI Ethics Policy, aligned with internationally recognized frameworks including UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) AI Principles. A defined oversight structure, supported by a dedicated AI ethics office, provides oversight, escalation paths, and accountability across the AI portfolio at SAP. An external advisory panel is consulted to deepen the understanding of broader ethical implications where necessary. SAP applies a structured AI ethics impact assessment to classify use cases by risk and determine the appropriate review path. High-risk use cases are reviewed through defined governance bodies, with escalation to the AI ethics steering committee and, when broader implications arise, the Executive Board of SAP SE. When no ethically acceptable trade-off can be identified, the AI system cannot proceed in that form. Clear ethical principles, accountable oversight, and structured review define the boundaries within which agents can operate.

SAP governs both internal AI use and AI delivered through its products to ensure regulatory compliance. All AI use cases undergo risk classification; high-risk systems apply continuous monitoring, human oversight, data governance, and accuracy controls. Third-party components are governed through due diligence and ongoing compliance checks. SAP certifies its AI against international standards aligned with the International Organization for Standardization and the National Institute of Standards and Technology, supporting customers with the documentation required for their own compliance obligations. With trust, integration, and governance in place, the AI-native enterprise opens beyond SAP.

AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP The platform layer is where applications, agents, and workflows run. SAP Business AI Platform, which includes SAP Business Technology Platform, provides composable services across data management, application development, integration, and security. Workloads are defined declaratively. Infrastructure, dependencies, and deployment targets are captured as configuration rather than code, so the interface stays stable while the platform evolves underneath. An AI Golden Path for application development - built on SAP Cloud Application Programming Model, the ABAP Cloud development model (ABAP RESTful application programming model), and the SAP Fiori design system - delivers consistent data models, harmonized APIs, and unified lifecycle management. With proven scalability supporting millions of tenants globally, the platform delivers the reliability, performance, sustainability, and security required for enterprise-scale AI. The shift from AI-first to AI-native expands the platform beyond building and running applications and providing integration. It now supports both deterministic applications and adaptive agents on the same multi-cloud foundation, managing the full lifecycle of agents, specifically their operational aspects, such as deployment, runtime, security, compliance, and observability. SAP Business AI Platform's multi-cloud capabilities allow deployment of the same agent to multiple providers, and even to sovereign and private cloud environments, with the platform ensuring consistent enterprise qualities such as reliability, scalability, and compliance across infrastructures.
documents.s: Platform Layer: Managed Agent Runtime at Scale

documents.t: SAP Business AI Platform provides a managed agent runtime to run enterprise agents reliably at scale. When an agent is created, the platform supplies essential harness capabilities such as security, observability, tenant isolation, sandboxing, and persistent memory. The model reasons. The harness connects. The platform governs. Research shows that the same model performs dramatically differently depending on the system around it. The harness, not the model, determines the ceiling. In practice, the platform is designed to provide standardized software development kits for building agents, an agent sandbox for safe development and testing, container-hosted execution, an agent skills registry for discovering reusable capabilities, and continuous agent evaluations for quality assurance. Each customer’s context, memory, and reasoning artifacts are strictly separated from day one, following the platform’s proven tenancy isolation patterns. Extensibility is built in from the start. Customers and partners customize agents without modifying the underlying code through four patterns: tool extensibility through the Model Context Protocol, skills as reusable building blocks, pre and post extension hooks and instructions that precondition the agent’s behavior with domain knowledge and operating guidelines. For agents that support extensions, developers define what customers can change and where customer logic can run. Customers can build and deploy those extensions separately from the agent itself. Observability is built on OpenTelemetry, covering agent execution end to end with traces, logs, and metrics. With transparent tracking of model calls and resource consumption, enterprises gain visibility into AI costs and adoption, and data to help assess financial and environmental impacts. Agent identifiers and execution traces connect usage to the agent, the work it performed, and the outcome. A platform that runs autonomous agents must also govern them. As agents start to act across systems and organizational boundaries, SAP treats trust, security, and integration as architectural prerequisites, embedded into the platform by design.

AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP The process layer is where business logic is defined and where the shift from rigid, predefined paths to agent-enabled orchestration takes shape. A simple request, such as hiring third-party developers, can involve procurement, legal, finance, IT, and supplier management, each with its own systems and approval chains. End-user workflows are constantly evolving and increasingly complex, spanning multiple stakeholders across heterogeneous landscapes. The AI-native architecture transforms how business processes are executed, from logic embedded in applications into a model in which applications, workflows, integration, and agents collaborate to deliver outcomes. The shift from AI-first to AI-native redefines how process logic is structured and executed. In the AI-first model, AI assists process execution within application boundaries: automating steps and suggesting actions but scoped to individual products. In the AI-native model, applications become capability providers, exposing stable APIs, events, and data that agents can discover and invoke. This enables business-process innovation through a deliberate mix: AI handles tasks requiring complex reasoning, while deterministic execution helps ensure reliability for specific processes. Both paths extend the reach of the system of context across the enterprise. Agents follow a reason-act-observe loop to decompose goals, execute actions using tools, and refine based on results. Execution can be optimized through scheduling and reuse strategies that minimize redundant inference and improve overall efficiency. Work can begin with a conversation, business event, or a schedule, and the same access and audit controls apply in each case. When an agent needs approval or more information, the platform routes the request through an active conversation or a tracked task in the responsible person's inbox. The agent can pause until a response arrives. Agents are organized by business domain, not by individual systems. A procurement agent, for example, orchestrates across ERP, sourcing, supplier management, and third-party systems as a single domain-aware participant. To deliver this, agents need a consistent way to be created, tested, and deployed.
documents.s: Process Layer: Agentic Orchestration & Joule Studio

documents.t: SAP supports building solutions across the determinism-autonomy spectrum: deterministic apps and workflows for predictable control flow, bounded agents with defined toolsets and guardrails, and open-ended agents for complex reasoning with broader autonomy. Where a task belongs on this spectrum is a design decision, and most solutions combine several points. Code-based agents can be built directly with a standardized agent software development kit or generated from natural-language intent through assisted authoring (Intent Based Development) in Joule Studio. Both paths produce portable, version-controlled code that can be built and reviewed with standard developer tools (IDEs, text editors, and terminals) or Joule Studio in the browser and deployed to the same agent runtime. Agent Skills complement these agents. A skill packages instructions and supporting resources (such as tools) that Joule or another agent loads into its context when needed. Because skills can express instructions in natural language, domain experts can contribute their knowledge without implementing a complete agent. Skills suit conversational work with many variations and knowledge reused across agents. Code-based agents run with their own context and interfaces, and manage their execution and state, making them suitable for high-volume tasks and flows requiring precise control. The two approaches can be combined. Agents built in Joule Studio are moving toward a skill-based model: a generic, managed agent harness runs the reasoning loop and loads the agent's skills and tools, started for each request and scaled down when idle. Even then, as much logic as possible belongs in tools, because code is cheaper and deterministic, while skills carry only the judgment that needs a language model. However, real business scenarios rarely involve building and deploying a single agent. A procurement solution, for example, combines an application for purchase requisitions, an approval workflow for spend authorization, and one or more agents for supplier selection and contract compliance. These components are managed as a single deployable solution with a shared lifecycle and dependencies. All of this comes together in Joule Studio, the unified design-time environment for building agents and agentic solutions. For rapid prototyping, developers can go straight from intent to code. Customers can start with intent views and change to code views and tools without rearchitecting, following SAP's AI Golden Path, which provides comprehensive guidance, from foundation services through agent development to production deployment. For production solutions, the flow progresses from business intent through a product requirements document, specifications, and code generation to deployment, with process knowledge (SAP Signavio), landscape data (SAP LeanIX), and domain models (SAP Knowledge Graph) from SAP informing each stage. All these documents for intent, product requirements and specifications and the code are generated by AI but can be reviewed and altered by the user at every stage. The documents contain the generated proposal for a solution to the business problem posed in the original intent prompt of the user. The solution and its assets, whether these are agents, workflows, apps, already existing SAP standard tools or all of them combined, are derived from the business context knowledge from the above mentioned products. The same approach extends to transformation and migration. In the AI-first model, moving from legacy to cloud is human led and labor intensive. In the AI-native model, agents accelerate code migration, data transformation, and test automation, reducing modernization time, risk, and downtime. Trust and governance for agent interactions, including agent identity, open protocol standards, and governed integration, are detailed in the Integration, security, ethics, and governance section. The process layer defines how applications and agents are modeled and built. The foundation layer powers them with data, reasoning, and memory capabilities.
AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP
documents.s: The Resilient and Sovereign Cloud for AI Workloads

documents.t: The system of context, the ecosystem, and the agents that operate within them are only as valuable as the infrastructure they run on. An AI-native enterprise runs on an intelligent, resilient cloud that delivers reliable, scalable performance worldwide. The cloud strategy at SAP balances latency, sustainability, compliance, and cost through a multitier deployment model: Public cloud provides shared, multitenant infrastructure at economies of scale. Private cloud offers single-tenant models with maximum flexibility. SAP Sovereign Cloud offerings help organizations adopt cloud technologies while maintaining control over their data, infrastructure, and compliance in line with local laws and regulations, including the use of compliant large language models. SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site offerings provide sovereign cloud capabilities within a customer’s selected or owned data centers.
documents.s: Multitier deployment - public, private and sovereign cloud

documents.t: Cloud solutions are designed to be ethical, secure, reliable, scalable, sustainable, and cost-optimized, with high availability supported by standardized resilience patterns, near-zero downtime maintenance, and disaster recovery across regions. Portability across infrastructure environments reduces vendor lock-in and enables workload relocation across platforms and countries. Elasticity allows applications and agents to scale automatically with demand, containerized for fast startup and fine-grained horizontal scaling, reducing environmental impact by avoiding idle resource consumption. AI-enabled operations provide automated anomaly detection, predictive issue resolution, and self-healing workflows - moving from reactive incident management to proactive, intelligent operations and reducing operational expenses and energy waste. Standardized observability based on OpenTelemetry covers agents and applications comprehensively, capturing not only operational health but also metering and compliance with audit logs for what agents do, how they reason, where they act, and whom they call. This data serves a dual purpose: it keeps operations reliable and becomes a feedback signal for continuous agent improvement, adding to the context that informs future reasoning and decisioning. The SAP Cloud ALM solution extends from application-centric to AI-aware operations, supporting customers with the tools and insights needed to operate AI scenarios reliably at scale. SAP advances sustainable cloud operations through a multilayered infrastructure strategy that reduces the environmental impact of data centers, in line with the global environmental policy. This includes running 100% of SAP-owned data centers on renewable energy, optimizing workloads, and collaborating closely with cloud infrastructure suppliers to help ensure their services and hardware align with the sustainability strategy at SAP. Operating at scale serves every customer. Differentiated value is created where each customer’s context is unique, and that is the role of customer-specific development services.

AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP Today, users navigate between applications, follow predefined workflows, and manually piece together information across systems to get work done. AI-native experiences are assembled dynamically, surfacing relevant information and actions specific to each user’s intent, context, and goals, rather than being statically designed and delivered to serve the majority. This requires a fundamental shift in how we design and deliver the user experience. Users will no longer navigate to applications but simply state intent, and the system assembles the experience around them. The UX layer brings together three tiers: The design layer is the Compositional Design System - the foundational layer that enables the capabilities of the other experience layers. It is built from two parts: (1) an agent and services - including intent analysis, planning, component selection, generation, and rendering - and (2) a catalogue of assets. The catalogue contains composites: flexible, scalable components made up of primitives, such as buttons, text, boxes, and circles. The catalogue further includes design knowledge: guidance on how composites can be modified and in what contexts they should be used, alongside general design knowledge encoding the enterprise qualities SAP delivers at scale - accessibility, product standards, globalization, and compliance - together with institutional design best practices built throughout the system. The intelligence layer makes experiences context-aware and trustworthy. It powers conversation, voice, and multimodal interaction - letting users express intent naturally across any modality. It also defines how users stay in control: through transparency, agency, and privacy boundaries that make AI assistance feel safe and predictable rather than opaque. The engagement layer, Joule Work, unifies the design and intelligence layers into a single entry point that interprets user intent, surfaces the right insights, automates routine work, and coordinates AI agents and workflows across the enterprise - enabling people to focus on the decisions that move the business forward, within guardrails they control. Joule Work extends across multiple modalities - desktop, web, mobile, in-car, and more - with transparency and privacy by design. Voice AI makes applications as natural as having a conversation. Physical AI also extends Joule into robotics and smart glasses. Joule Work structures these experiences into five experience modes, each serving a particular intent and purpose for users: Discover surfaces AI-prioritized tasks, alerts, and opportunities from across connected systems so users can act directly, continue in a Conversation, or open a Space. Conversations is where users express intent and explore outcomes through continuous dialogue across SAP. Spaces are dynamic workspaces assembled on the fly, bringing together the right data, tools, and context for a specific goal. Jobs make agentic work traceable for the business user, automating routine tasks within defined guardrails and escalating to humans for key decisions or missing information. Develop gives builders the tools to create and deploy agentic solutions using Joule Studio's AI-first development environment, connecting them to SAP's business context, data, and interfaces to build solutions grounded in real business processes. Joule Work is delivered as a service managed by SAP. This enables continuous improvement of the experience, delivering innovation without additional effort for customers. Embedded insights from the SAP Analytics Cloud solution bring real-time visibility. When results carry semantic information - measures, dimensions, and visualization hints - the design layer determines how to present them. The same semantic specification renders through native components on web, desktop, and mobile. Together, these capabilities create experiences that explain what happened and why it matters, then recommend the next action, helping users move smoothly from data to decision. This NorthStar applies to agentic and AI-native interaction patterns. It complements, not replaces, SAP application experiences. While the experience layer allows users to articulate their needs, translating those intentions into tangible business outcomes demands a sophisticated orchestration of applications, intelligent agents, and interconnected business logic, which is the role of the process layer.
documents.s: AI-native User Experience Layer with Joule Work

documents.t: AI-native North Star architecture Last updated on Oct 23, 2026 by SAP The AI-native architecture from SAP rests on three simple premises: Models that reason are the baseline. Context, which grounds AI in business data and semantics, is what makes reasoning and its results relevant to the business. Agents and Assistants that plan, act, and learn turn this into outcomes. The four architectural layers that make up the AI-native North Star architecture from SAP deliver all three. The four layers are as follows: The user experience layer evolves from static to adaptive. Joule becomes the central engagement layer across the SAP Autonomous Suite, shifting interaction from app navigation to intent-driven execution: instead of navigating across several applications, a user states the goal, such as resolving a customer's disputed invoice, and Joule carries out the steps across applications, in whichever channel the user is working in. Interfaces become contextual, multimodal, and generative. The process layer evolves from predefined to agentic. The business logic, rules, and data that applications have traditionally embodied become capabilities that agents plan and execute across SAP, partner, and third-party systems, with every call routed through a governed gateway. A unified design-time environment supports building both applications and agents from business intent to production. The foundation layer evolves from a system of record to a system of context. SAP Business Data Cloud provides governed data, SAP Knowledge Graph links it to business meaning, and decision traces record why past decisions were made. That connected context is what turns data into enterprise intelligence: agents can reason about why things happen, not only what happened. The platform layer evolves from hosting applications to running SAP-managed enterprise agents integrated across the customer landscape. The platform provides runtime, sandbox, observability, and governance to build and operate reliable enterprise agents on top of stateless AI models. Agent lifecycle, identity, routing, and integration are built into the platform.

The experience layer generates context from each user interaction. The process layer extends it across the landscape by connecting applications, APIs, events, and business capabilities, allowing agents to reason across them. The foundation layer stores and compounds this into institutional knowledge. The platform layer runs and protects it at enterprise scale. Trust governs how this context flows across all four layers.
documents.s: How each layer plays a distinct role in the system of context

documents.t: The four layers work together in each user interaction. Users switch between applications to verify data, follow up on issues, and complete processes. With an AI-native architecture, this becomes a connected, outcome-first flow in which the system not only identifies issues but also resolves them within defined business policies. As an example, a finance analyst asks Joule to "resolve high-value disputes likely to delay payment and minimize impact on days' sales outstanding (DSO)." Joule routes the request to an agent that spans sales, ERP, and service management, with the authority to analyze, decide, and execute resolution workflows within governed boundaries. The agent queries SAP Knowledge Graph to discover the right APIs and data products, retrieves disputes across applications that previously lacked a shared access layer, and draws on decision traces from past resolutions: which escalation paths worked, which settlement patterns reduced DSO, and which customers responded to which approaches. The agent identifies high-risk disputes, selects optimal resolution strategies based on historical outcomes, executes follow-ups such as customer communication and internal escalations, and initiates resolution workflows. Only exceptions or policy-bound decisions are routed for human approval. As disputes are resolved, payment commitments are secured and tracked through to completion, helping ensure closure rather than partial progress. The results are a measurable reduction in DSO, faster dispute-resolution cycles, and higher recovery rates, with most cases resolved without manual intervention. The next time a similar dispute arises, the agent’s resolution strategies improve because it learned from this one. This is the system of context in action: SAP Knowledge Graph provides semantic grounding, decision traces from past resolutions inform execution, and each completed resolution feeds back as a verified outcome signal. The example above touched every layer of the architecture. The following sections examine each one.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 When you open a pull request against the SAP Architecture Center repository, a set of automated checks runs automatically. These are GitHub Actions workflows that read your changes and give you fast, friendly feedback, before a human maintainer ever looks at your contribution.
documents.s: Automated Checks for Architecture Center Contributions

documents.t: Think of the checks as an automated first reviewer. They catch the small, mechanical things (a misspelled product name, a missing front matter field, a dead link) so that you can fix them in seconds and the human reviewer can focus on what really matters: the quality and clarity of your reference architecture. A few things worth knowing up front: The checks are here to help, not to get in your way. Most issues they report take moments to fix, and the feedback points you straight at the file and line. You do not need to install anything. Everything runs in GitHub when you push. If you contribute through our no-code Quick Start editor, the same checks still run on the pull request it opens for you. A failing check is normal. It simply means something needs a small adjustment. Push a new commit and the checks run again automatically. info New to contributing? Start with the community introduction and the contribution process first, then come back here to understand the checks you'll see on your pull request.
documents.s: What the checks do for you

documents.t: The checks report their findings in three places, so you'll never have to go searching: Inline annotations on the Files changed tab: comments pinned to the exact line that needs attention (for example, the spelling and typo checks mark the offending word right where it appears). The Checks tab: one entry per check, each with a green tick, a red cross, or a neutral note, plus a detailed log and a per-job summary you can expand. One sticky pull request comment titled 🔎 Content check results: a single, continuously-updated comment that gathers the content findings grouped by check. It rebuilds itself every time a check finishes, so it always reflects your latest commit (look for the footer noting the commit it was updated for). note The sticky comment aggregates the content checks that can block a merge (internal links, external links, SEO front matter, front matter properties, reference architecture IDs, Draw.io files, orphan files), and it shows their blocking errors only. Spelling, typos, grammar, and the H1 title check are deliberately not repeated in the comment: spelling, typos, and the H1 title check annotate inline on the Files changed tab, right next to the line in question, and grammar posts its advisory notes on the Checks tab. Non-blocking warnings, such as an SEO length just outside the recommended range, stay inline and in the job summary, not in this comment. For a full, example-driven walkthrough of what each surface looks like and how to resolve what you find, see Errors & Warnings.

The table below indexes every content check. "Blocking?" tells you whether a failure must be resolved before the pull request can merge. Follow the Learn more link for the detail page on each check. Check What it verifies Blocking? Learn more Spelling Every word in your Markdown is spelled correctly, using cspell plus the project's custom dictionaries. Yes Spelling Typos Common typos and misspellings, caught by the fast typos checker. Yes Typos Grammar Prose style and grammar, via LanguageTool. Advisory only. No Grammar Front Matter Properties Changed reference architecture pages credit their author, carry a fresh date, and keep the house-style default fields. Yes Front Matter Properties H1 Title Pages take their title from the front matter, so Markdown bodies must not contain a level-1 # heading. Yes H1 Title SEO Front Matter The title and description lengths sit in the search-engine-friendly range. Yes* SEO Front Matter Reference Architecture IDs Each reference architecture carries a valid, unique six-character id and a matching slug. Yes Reference Architecture IDs Internal Links No links point to SAP-internal-only hosts that would break for public visitors. Yes Internal Links External Links Links pointing to the public web are reachable, checked with lychee. Yes External Links Draw.io Files Diagram files stay under 1 MB and embed their images (no external references). Yes Draw.io Files Orphan Files Images, diagrams, and other assets you add are actually referenced somewhere. Yes* Orphan Files tip Grammar is the only check that never blocks a merge. Treat its notes as a friendly proofreader's second opinion. A couple of checks marked Yes* can also emit non-blocking warnings alongside their blocking errors: SEO Front Matter warns when a length is merely outside the recommended range, and Orphan Files warns when an asset is referenced only outside its own reference architecture folder. See each check's page for the detail.
documents.s: The content checks at a glance

documents.t: Technical writing is full of words that no general dictionary knows, such as product names, acronyms, partner brands, and the names of people. So the spell checker is taught the project's vocabulary through four custom dictionaries: sap : SAP product and solution names industry : general technology and industry terms partners : partner and vendor names people : contributor and author names If the Spelling check flags a word that is genuinely correct, the fix is usually to add it to the right dictionary rather than to change your text. The dictionaries are plain text files, one word per line, so updating them is easy. tip See Custom Dictionaries for exactly which file to edit, how the four dictionaries are organised, and how to add a new term.

Alongside the content checks, a second group of workflows keeps the site itself healthy: building and deploying the site, scanning for security issues, and verifying open-source license compliance. These run largely in the background and are not something you normally act on as a content contributor, but it's good to know they exist. See Operational Workflows for a tour of what runs behind the scenes.

tip Most checks are path-filtered: they only run when files relevant to them change. Edit a Markdown page and you'll see the spelling, typo, link, and front matter checks; touch a .drawio diagram and the Draw.io check runs. The checks run on pull requests targeting the dev (and main) branches, so you only ever see the checks that actually apply to your change, with no distractions. This keeps feedback focused: a small text fix won't trigger diagram validation, and a diagram-only change won't run the grammar linter. When you're ready to start resolving findings, go to Errors & Warnings for concrete examples.
documents.s: Which checks run on my pull request?

documents.t: Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 Reference architectures are full of words no general-purpose spell checker has ever seen: SAP product names, cloud and AI acronyms, partner brands, and the names and GitHub handles of the people who write them. Custom dictionaries are how we teach our spell checker that these words are correct, so it only flags the mistakes that actually matter.
documents.s: Custom Spelling Dictionaries in the Architecture Center

documents.t: A standard English dictionary knows architecture and deployment. It does not know BTP, Datasphere, OAuth, Snowflake, or a contributor handle like fabianleh. Without a curated word list, the spell checker would underline every single one of these as a mistake, drowning the one real typo in a sea of false positives. Nobody would trust the check, and everybody would learn to ignore it. The custom dictionaries fix that. They are the project's shared vocabulary: an agreed-upon taxonomy of the specialised words that legitimately appear in our content. When you add a term once, it is accepted everywhere, for everyone, forever. Non-developers welcome Editing a dictionary means adding one word to a plain text file. There is no code to run and nothing to compile. If you can edit a Markdown page, you can add a word to a dictionary.

Spelling in the Architecture Center is guarded by two independent tools that do opposite things. Understanding the division of labour tells you exactly where a given word belongs. cspell is proactive. It is the taxonomy of valid words. cspell flags anything it does not recognise, so the custom dictionaries exist to list every specialised term we consider correct. This is the layer you extend most often. See Spelling. typos is reactive. It does not flag a word just for being unfamiliar. It only fires when a word closely resembles a known misspelling (for example teh for the). Because of that, SAP, industry, and partner names almost never trip it. See Typos. The practical consequence: when a valid term gets flagged, which check flagged it tells you which file to edit. cspell flagging an unknown word means it belongs in a .cspell dictionary. typos "correcting" a real word means it belongs in the typos word list. note These two checks are complementary, not redundant. cspell catches unknown words; typos catches plausible-looking words that are actually wrong (recieve, occured). Running both gives broad coverage without either one becoming too noisy.

All of the spelling configuration lives in cspell.json at the repository root. Here is the shape of it: { "version": "0.2", "language": "en,en-US,en-GB", "dictionaryDefinitions": [ { "name": "sap", "path": ".cspell/sap.txt", "addWords": true }, { "name": "industry", "path": ".cspell/industry.txt", "addWords": true }, { "name": "partners", "path": ".cspell/partners.txt", "addWords": true }, { "name": "people", "path": ".cspell/people.txt", "addWords": true } ], "dictionaries": ["sap", "industry", "partners", "people"], "words": ["RAXXXX", "claudeignore", "Conv", "Ashburn", "gingershot"], "ignoreRegExpList": ["Urls", "Email", "HexValues", "FrontMatterTags", "..."], "ignorePaths": ["**/node_modules/**", "**/*.drawio", "..."], "files": ["docs/**/*.md", "docs/**/*.mdx", "news/**/*.md", "news/**/*.mdx"] } The pieces that matter to a contributor: dictionaryDefinitions registers each of the four custom word lists and gives it a name. addWords: true means these are the lists the project treats as its own extendable vocabulary. dictionaries switches those four lists on for the whole project. words is an inline array for a handful of true one-offs that do not fit any category: currently RAXXXX, claudeignore, Conv, Ashburn, and gingershot. Use the .cspell files for anything that has a natural category; reserve this inline list for genuine oddities. ignoreRegExpList and patterns tell cspell to skip things that are not prose: Urls, Email addresses, HexValues (colour codes), and several front-matter fields such as tags, contributors, author, id, and slug. That is why you never need to add a URL or a slug to a dictionary. ignorePaths excludes whole paths from spell checking, including node_modules, binary and diagram assets (*.drawio, *.svg, *.png, …), the RA0000 template, the cookie-and-privacy pages, and the team page. files scopes the check to Markdown under docs/ and news/ only.

Each dictionary has a clear theme. Picking the right one keeps the shared vocabulary organised and easy to review. All four use the same simple format: case-insensitive, one term per line, and # to start a comment. (The addWords: true flag that makes them extendable lives on each entry in cspell.json, not in the text files themselves.) Dictionary File What belongs here Example terms Rough size SAP .cspell/sap.txt SAP acronyms, product names, and SAP-specific terms BTP, HANA, ABAP, Fiori, Kyma ~77 terms Industry .cspell/industry.txt General cloud, architecture, and AI acronyms and terms (not SAP- or vendor-specific) OAuth, OIDC, gRPC ~177 terms Partners .cspell/partners.txt Partner and competitor names, plus their products and technologies AWS, Azure, Snowflake, Kafka ~96 terms People .cspell/people.txt Contributor names and GitHub handles that appear in prose and bylines author names and handles ~120 terms Keep the taxonomy clean The categories exist for a reason. A SAP product goes in sap.txt, a protocol like SAML goes in industry.txt, a vendor like Databricks goes in partners.txt, and a person goes in people.txt. Do not dump everything into one file. A tidy taxonomy is far easier to review and keep correct.

When cspell flags a valid term, adding it is three quick steps: Choose the right dictionary by category, using the table above. Add the term on its own line in that file. Order is not critical, but keeping it near related entries (under the existing # section comments) helps reviewers. Commit the change alongside the content that uses the word, so the check passes in the same pull request. For example, to teach cspell a new SAP service, you would add one line to .cspell/sap.txt: # Platform & core BTP HANA + BuildApps That is the entire change. Because the match is case-insensitive, you do not need to list btp, BTP, and Btp separately. One entry covers them all. One word per line Do not put multiple terms on a single line or separate them with commas. cspell reads each line as one entry, so AWS, Azure would be treated as a single (never-matching) token. Give each term its own line.

The reactive check is configured in _typos.toml at the repository root. You should rarely touch it. Add an entry only when typos wrongly "corrects" a real term, not just because a word is unfamiliar (that is cspell's job). To allow a word, map it to itself under [default.extend-words], and keep the keys lowercase: [default.extend-words] advices = "advices" # "remittance advices", a valid accounting term rto = "rto" # Recovery Time Objective alo = "alo" # At-Least-Once (delivery QoS) aks = "aks" # Azure Kubernetes Service aci = "aci" # Azure Container Instance The same file also has a [files] section with extend-exclude, which lists path and file patterns typos skips entirely, for example *.min.js, *.lock, *.svg, *.drawio, and the docs/ref-arch/RA0000/ template (its Latin placeholder text would otherwise trip the check). Keep it small and reactive The typos list is intentionally short. If a word is simply specialised and unknown, it belongs in a .cspell dictionary, not here. Only genuine false "corrections" earn a line in _typos.toml.

The decision in one line Is cspell flagging a valid word? Add it to the matching .cspell list: SAP, industry, partners, or people. Is typos wrongly correcting a valid word? Add it (mapped to itself, lowercase) to _typos.toml. One more thing worth remembering: the team page (docs/community/10-the-team.md) and the cookie-and-privacy page are excluded wholesale via ignorePaths in cspell.json. So people.txt only needs the names and handles that appear outside those two pages: in article prose, bylines, and front-matter examples.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 Diagrams are a core part of every reference architecture, and they ship as .drawio files committed right next to your Markdown. When your pull request adds or changes any .drawio file, this workflow runs two quick checks on just the files you touched, making sure each diagram is small enough to load fast and fully self-contained. Only your changed files are checked This check compares your branch against the pull request base and looks only at .drawio files you added, modified, or renamed. Diagrams that already live in the repository and that you did not touch are left alone. If your PR changes no .drawio files at all, the workflow reports "nothing to check" and passes.
documents.s: Draw.io File Checks for Size and External Images

documents.t: # Check Rule Annotation title 1 File size A .drawio file must be at most 1024 KB (1 MB) drawio size 2 External images A .drawio file must not reference external images (image=http...) drawio external image Both checks run independently, so a single file can be flagged by one, the other, or both.

Every changed .drawio file is measured. If it exceeds 1024 KB, the check fails and reports the file's measured size so you know how far over the limit you are. ❌ docs/ref-arch/.../my-diagram.drawio is too large (1337 KB). Maximum allowed size is 1024 KB. Diagrams usually grow past the limit when raster images (screenshots, exported PNG files, logos) are pasted directly into the canvas. A compact, vector-based diagram comfortably stays well under a megabyte. Keeping diagrams small Prefer the built-in SAP and technology shapes over pasted screenshots. Crop and compress any bitmap image before embedding it. If a diagram is genuinely large, split it into focused sub-diagrams. This is usually clearer for readers, too.

A .drawio file must not point to images hosted somewhere else on the web. The check scans each changed file for an external image reference (an image=http... entry) and fails if it finds one. ❌ docs/ref-arch/.../my-diagram.drawio contains external image references (image=http). External images are not allowed in drawio files. Please embed the image directly. Images must be embedded directly in the diagram (stored inline as base64 data) rather than linked by URL. Embedding keeps every diagram: Self-contained: the file carries everything it needs. Reliable: nothing breaks when a remote URL moves, expires, or goes offline. Free of external dependencies: no request leaves the reader's browser to a third-party host, which also avoids privacy concerns. How external links get in Draw.io can insert an external reference when you paste an image by URL, or drag an image in from a browser tab instead of from a local file. If you always add images from a local file (or copy-paste the pixels), draw.io embeds them for you.

Both checks are blocking: a failure keeps the pull request from being merged until it is resolved. Results show up in three places: Annotations attached to the offending file, titled drawio size and drawio external image. They carry no line number, so they appear on the Checks tab and at the top of the file on the Files changed tab, rather than against a specific line. A "Check drawio Files" section in the sticky summary comment the PR check bot posts on your PR. A job summary on the workflow run, listing each flagged file with its measured size or the external-reference finding. warning A green run means the diagrams you changed are within limits and self-contained. It does not re-check diagrams you did not touch.

Finding Fix File too large Simplify or optimise the diagram, compress embedded bitmaps, or split it into smaller diagrams until it is under 1024 KB. External image reference Open the diagram, remove the linked image, and re-add it so it is embedded (base64) instead of referenced by URL. After you push the fix, the workflow re-runs automatically on the new commit. Once both checks pass, the "Check drawio Files" section turns green. Diagramming guide For the full conventions on creating and editing diagrams (naming, theming, light and dark variants, and export), see the diagramming guide.

This is one of several automated checks that run on your contributions. See the Automated Checks overview for the full picture, and the companion pages: Spelling and Custom Dictionaries Typos and Grammar Front Matter Properties and SEO Front Matter Reference Architecture IDs Internal Links and External Links Orphan Files Operational Workflows What errors and warnings mean on your PR New to contributing? Start with the community intro, the contribution process, and, for a new reference architecture, the no-code Quick Start editor.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 You have opened your pull request. Now what? This page walks through exactly what happens next: which checks run, where their results appear, which ones can hold up a merge, and how to read and fix each message with concrete examples. If you have not yet met the individual checks, the Overview introduces them one by one.
documents.s: What Happens When PR Checks Find Errors or Warnings

documents.t: As soon as you open a pull request against dev (or main), or push a new commit to it, GitHub starts the relevant checks. Two things are worth knowing from the start: The checks are path-filtered. Each one only runs when the files it cares about actually changed. Edit a single Markdown page and you will not trigger the Draw.io check; add an image and the spelling check stays quiet. You only ever see feedback that is relevant to what you touched. Results arrive within a few minutes. The checks run in parallel. Most finish in well under five minutes, and each one reports as soon as it is done, so you do not have to wait for all of them before fixing the first problem. tip Contributing through the no-code Quick Start editor? The same checks run on the pull request it opens for you. Everything on this page applies in exactly the same way; you just read the results on GitHub.
documents.s: What happens the moment you open or update a PR

documents.t: The checks never leave you searching. Findings land in one (or more) of three surfaces, and every check also writes an expandable job summary under its entry on the Checks tab. Where you look What you find there Checks that report here Files changed tab: inline annotations pinned to the exact line A speech-bubble comment next to the offending word, link, or front matter field Typos, Spelling, Internal Links, SEO Front Matter, Front Matter Properties, Reference Architecture IDs, Draw.io Files, Orphan Files Checks tab: one entry per check Status (tick / cross / note), full run log, and a job summary Grammar (and every other check also writes a job summary here) One sticky PR comment titled 🔎 Content check results Findings grouped by check, rebuilt on every run Internal Links, SEO Front Matter, Front Matter Properties, Reference Architecture IDs, Draw.io Files, Orphan Files, External Links A few deliberate details about the sticky comment: Typos and Spelling are not in it. They annotate inline on the Files changed tab only, right next to the word in question, which is the fastest place to fix them. Grammar is not in it either. Grammar suggestions appear on the Checks tab. It is idempotent. The comment rebuilds its entire body every time a check finishes, so it always reflects your latest commit. Look for the footer line noting the commit it was updated for. It works on fork pull requests. The comment is assembled in the base repository's context and never checks out your PR's code, so it can post results even for contributions from a fork, without ever running your changes with a writable token. It shows blocking errors only. A non-blocking warning (for example an SEO length outside the recommended range, or an asset referenced only outside its RA folder) appears inline on the Files changed tab and in the job summary, not in this comment. A check that reports only warnings still shows as a pass here. info If a check does not appear in the sticky comment at all, that usually means its paths did not match your changes, so it never ran. That is normal and expected, not a failure.

Not every finding stops a merge. Some are hard gates; others are friendly suggestions. Here is the split. Blocking: fails the check and holds the merge Non-blocking: a warning you should weigh, but which never fails the build Typos: any typo in changed Markdown Grammar: always advisory, by design Spelling: any unknown word SEO Front Matter: a value merely outside the recommended range SEO Front Matter: a value past the hard bounds Orphan Files: an asset referenced only outside its own RA directory Front Matter Properties: any missing/non-conforming field Reference Architecture IDs: bad id or slug Internal Links: any SAP-internal-only host External Links: any broken external URL Draw.io Files: oversized file or external image reference Orphan Files: an asset referenced nowhere note The SEO and Orphan Files checks each sit on both sides of the line. SEO fails only when a title or description blows past the hard minimum/maximum; a value that is merely shorter or longer than the ideal range is a warning. Orphan Files fails only when an asset is referenced nowhere; an asset referenced only outside its RA folder is a warning (it might legitimately be shared).

Imagine a single PR that adds a new reference architecture and manages to trip almost everything at once. Here is each problem, the message you would see, and the one-line fix. (All values below are illustrative.)
documents.s: A pull request with nine problems

documents.t: You wrote integreation instead of integration. docs/ref-arch/RA1234/readme.md:12:5 - Unknown word (integreation) An inline annotation lands on that word on the Files changed tab, titled Spelling (and Typos flags common slips like this too). Fix: correct the spelling. See Spelling and Typos.

Your architecture legitimately mentions a brand-new SAP product, but cspell has never heard of it, so it reports it as an unknown word, the same shape of message as above. Fix: this is not a typo, so do not change the text. Add the term to the project dictionary at .cspell/sap.txt (one word per line) and commit that too. The next run will accept it. See Custom Dictionaries. tip The custom dictionaries are how the project teaches cspell every SAP-specific name: products, acronyms, service names. When a correct term is flagged, the fix is almost always "add it to the dictionary," never "reword the sentence." The Custom Dictionaries page explains which file to use.
documents.s: 2. A valid new product name flagged by cspell

documents.t: Your front matter title runs to 72 characters. The hard maximum is 65. docs/ref-arch/RA1234/readme.md:4: title is way too long (72 characters, hard maximum 65; recommended 40-60 characters). This is a blocking error (past the hard bound). Fix: tighten the title into the recommended 40–60 character range. Had it been, say, 63 characters, you would have seen a non-blocking warning instead. See SEO Front Matter.

You forgot to add yourself to contributors, and the last_update.date is from last month. docs/ref-arch/RA1234/readme.md: contributors is missing or does not include the PR author. docs/ref-arch/RA1234/readme.md: last_update.date is older than 7 days before today. Both are blocking. Fix: add your GitHub login to contributors, set last_update.author to your login, and bump last_update.date to today. See Front Matter Properties and the general front matter guide.

Your readme has id: ra1234 but slug: /ref-arch/ra9999. SLUG MISMATCH slug "/ref-arch/ra9999" != "/ref-arch/ra1234" -> docs/ref-arch/RA1234/readme.md The id must be exactly six lowercase letters/digits, and the slug must be /ref-arch/<id>. Fix: make the slug match the id (/ref-arch/ra1234). See Reference Architecture IDs.

You linked to an internal wiki that external visitors cannot reach. See the [internal design note](https://wiki.example-internal.invalid/display/ARCH/notes). docs/ref-arch/RA1234/readme.md:40: Internal-only SAP link (breaks for external visitors): https://wiki.example-internal.invalid/... (The .invalid host above is a stand-in. On a real PR this would be a host ending in one of the internal suffixes below. We never put a real internal host in content, including in examples.) The check flags any host matching *.tools.sap, *.int.sap, *.sap.corp, or sap.sharepoint.com. Fix: link to a public source instead, or remove the link. See Internal Links.
documents.s: 6. A link to an SAP-internal host

documents.t: One of your external links returns 404 Not Found. The check reports it in the job summary and in the sticky comment (not as an inline annotation, because broken links are often network-dependent and not tied to a changed line). ✗ https://example.com/this-page-moved | 404 Not Found Fix: update the URL or point it at a working page. See External Links.

You committed a diagram source file of about 1.4 MB. The limit is 1024 KB. ❌ docs/ref-arch/RA1234/diagram.drawio is too large (1434 KB). Maximum allowed size is 1024 KB. Fix: slim the diagram down: embedded raster images are the usual culprit. (The same check also fails on external image references inside a .drawio; images must be embedded, not linked.) See Draw.io Files and the diagramming guide.

You added architecture-overview.png but no page links to it. ❌ docs/ref-arch/RA1234/architecture-overview.png: Asset is not referenced in any Markdown file This is blocking. Fix: reference the image from your Markdown, or remove it if it is not needed. If the same image is instead referenced only from another RA's folder, you would get a non-blocking ⚠️ warning ("referenced only outside its RA directory") rather than an error. See Orphan Files.
documents.s: 9. An added image that nothing references

documents.t: There is nothing special to trigger: push a new commit to the same branch and the checks re-run automatically on your updated files. The sticky 🔎 Content check results comment updates in place (it does not pile up new comments), so you always read the latest state in one spot. info Contributing from a fork? GitHub hands fork pull requests a read-only token, so the Grammar suggestions cannot be posted to the Checks tab; they appear in the Actions run log instead. The aggregated content-check comment still posts normally, because it is built in the base repository's context. Everything else behaves the same.

You can relax: the checks are there to help. They exist to help your content meet the house style in seconds, long before a human reviewer weighs in on the ideas. Because almost every check is path-scoped, you only ever see feedback about the files you actually changed. And when every check shows a green tick and the sticky comment reads all clean, your pull request is ready for human review. For the big picture of how the whole system fits together, go back to the Overview. For the schedule-based and deployment workflows that run outside the PR flow, see Operational Workflows.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 When you add or edit a page, the links that point out to the wider web should still lead somewhere. The external link check verifies exactly that: it runs lychee against the Markdown you changed and flags any outbound link that no longer resolves.
documents.s: External Link Check for Broken Links with Lychee

documents.t: Whenever you open or update a pull request that touches Markdown (.md or .mdx) under docs/ or news/, this check collects the files you added, modified, or renamed and asks lychee to visit every external URL in them. If a link resolves, you hear nothing. If a link is dead, the check fails and tells you which one. The check only looks at the files in your diff, not the whole site. That keeps it fast and keeps the feedback focused on what you actually changed. info It also triggers when the workflow file itself (.github/workflows/check-ext-links.yml) changes, so maintainers can validate adjustments to the check safely.

Most checks in this suite (spelling, typos, internal links, front matter) are deterministic. They look at your text, find a problem on a specific line, and leave an inline annotation right there in the diff. External links are different. A link can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with your edit: the remote server is briefly down (a transient 5xx error), the server is rate-limiting the check (a 429 Too Many Requests), the URL moved or was retired since you first copied it. Because that breakage is network-dependent and often not tied to a particular changed line, this check does not post per-line annotations. Instead it writes its results to two places: Where What you see The job summary A full lychee report under the heading External links check The sticky PR comment A Check External Links section, aggregated alongside the other content checks So if you are looking for an external-link problem, look at the PR comment and the job summary rather than the inline diff.
documents.s: Why it reports differently from the local checks

documents.t: The check is configured to fail when a link is genuinely broken, so a dead URL will stop the PR from going green until it is fixed. A couple of details worth knowing: A 403 Forbidden is not reported. A 403 almost always means the target sits behind an authentication or login wall rather than that your link is broken, so the check treats it as reachable and never fails on it. Only a genuine breakage such as a 404 Not Found can block the PR. Transient failures are retried. lychee retries a failing link before giving up, so a brief network blip usually clears on its own. If a flaky 429 or 5xx response persists and fails the check, re-running it (see below) normally resolves it. A link that is genuinely broken stays failed until you fix it. It fails closed on odd filenames. As a safety measure, if a changed file path contains anything outside letters, digits, and the characters . _ / -, the check refuses to run and reports that instead. This is a security guard against unusual characters in paths from fork pull requests. In practice your file names will never trip this, so just name files normally. note If none of your changed Markdown lives under docs/ or news/, the check has nothing to look at and simply reports that there was nothing to check. That is a pass, not a problem.

Open the report. Find the Check External Links section in the sticky PR comment (or the External links check heading in the job summary) and read which URL failed and with what status. Decide if it is real or transient. A 404 Not Found means the page is genuinely gone, so you need to fix it. A 429 or a 5xx usually means the server was busy or briefly unavailable. A 403 is not reported at all, since it almost always indicates a login wall rather than a broken link. For a real break: correct the typo in the URL, or replace it with the current canonical address of the resource. If the resource is gone for good, link to an equivalent source or remove the link. For a transient failure: simply re-run the check. Rate limits and short outages normally clear, and a re-run often turns the check green with no change on your side. Re-running the check You can re-run a failed check from the PR's Checks tab on GitHub. See GitHub's docs on re-running workflows for the exact steps.

The best way to pass this check is to never add a fragile link in the first place. Prefer stable, canonical URLs Link to official, long-lived sources (a project's own documentation site, or its repository on github.com) rather than short-lived links such as URL shorteners, search-result pages, or temporary preview environments. Canonical URLs are far less likely to move or disappear, which keeps your page working long after you publish it. If you ever need to show an internal, non-public URL as an example in your prose, use an obviously fake placeholder (for instance, https://internal.example.com/your-resource) and say in the text that it is a placeholder. The check validates real links, and internal hosts are never reachable from the public CI runner.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 The Front Matter Properties check reads the front matter block at the top of every reference architecture (RA) page you touched in a pull request and makes sure it follows house style, and that it credits you and carries a fresh date. It is a blocking check: if a page drifts from the rules below, the check fails and the merge is held until you fix it. If you are new to front matter, read the front matter guide first. This page explains the automated rules that sit on top of it.
documents.s: Front Matter Properties Check for Reference Architectures

documents.t: The check runs on pull requests and inspects only the RA pages you actually changed, not the whole site. A page is in scope when all of the following are true: It lives under a four-digit RA folder: docs/ref-arch/RA####/ (for example docs/ref-arch/RA0042/). Its filename ends in .md or .mdx. It was added, modified, or renamed in your pull request (deleted files are ignored). Everything else is out of scope, including: The docs/ref-arch/RA0000/ demo and template page (deliberately excluded). Other docs such as docs/ref-arch/readme.md and the community guideline pages. News articles under news/. info Scope is computed from the diff between your branch and its base, so adding one small RA page will never drag unrelated pages into the check.
The check runs nine rules, split into two groups.

These six fields have sensible Docusaurus defaults. The check only complains when a field is present and set to the wrong value. If you leave a field out entirely, the default applies and the check stays quiet. Field Must be Why hide_table_of_contents false The on-page table of contents stays visible. hide_title false The page title renders from front matter. toc_min_heading_level 2 Matches the site default. toc_max_heading_level 4 Matches the site default. draft false A draft page is not deployed. unlisted false An unlisted page is hidden from navigation. tip The simplest way to stay green here is to copy the field values straight from the front matter guide and not change them.

These three fields credit the author and track freshness. Because an RA page should always name a person and carry a recent date, a missing value fails here too (unlike Group A). Field Fails when Notes contributors Missing or empty, or the pull request author is not in the list Compared case-insensitively against your GitHub login. last_update.date Missing, not a valid YYYY-MM-DD date, in the future, or more than 7 days old Keep it recent, and bump it when you edit the page. last_update.author Missing, or different from the pull request author Must be your GitHub login. warning The date rule has a 7-day freshness window. A last_update.date more than a week before the day the check runs is flagged, and a date in the future is flagged too. When you edit a page, set the date to the day you make the change. Maintainer exemption The repository maintainers cernus76, navyakhurana, julian-schambeck, and fabianleh are exempt from all three Group B authorship checks. This lets them make quick fixes on pages they did not author without changing authorship credit or update metadata. All six Group A default-value checks still apply to them.

When the check finds a problem, it reports in three places: Inline annotations on the Files changed tab of the pull request, pinned to the exact front matter line. A Check Front Matter Properties section in the sticky summary comment the PR check bot keeps on the pull request. A job summary on the check's run, listing how many pages were checked and how many errors were found. Each message names the file and the field, for example: docs/ref-arch/RA0042/readme.md:24 last_update.author `octocat` differs from the PR author `your-handle`.
documents.s: Where you will see the results

documents.t: Open the flagged page and align its front matter with the rules. A correct block looks like this. Replace your-handle with your own GitHub login and set the date to the day you are editing: --- # ... other fields ... hide_table_of_contents: false hide_title: false toc_min_heading_level: 2 toc_max_heading_level: 4 draft: false unlisted: false contributors: - your-handle last_update: author: your-handle date: 2026-10-15 --- Checklist: Add your GitHub handle to the contributors list (keep any existing contributors). Set last_update.author to your GitHub handle. Set last_update.date to today, in YYYY-MM-DD format. Leave the Group A fields at their expected values, or remove them to use the defaults. Push the fix to the same branch and the check re-runs automatically. For a full field-by-field reference, see the front matter guide. note These rules apply to authored reference architecture pages under docs/ref-arch/RA####/. They do not apply to community guideline pages like this one, so the author and date fields here follow a different convention.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 When you open a pull request, a grammar and prose check reads the English text in your changed pages and offers gentle suggestions: a stray double word, a missing comma, an awkward construction. It is powered by reviewdog and LanguageTool, and it complements the spell check rather than replacing it.
documents.s: Grammar and Prose Check with LanguageTool

documents.t: LanguageTool is a mature open-source proofreading engine. In our setup it runs bundled inside the reviewdog action's container image. There are no calls out to any external grammar API, so your prose never leaves the GitHub Actions runner. reviewdog then takes LanguageTool's findings and surfaces them where you can act on them. Think of it as a friendly editor reading over your shoulder: Spelling is handled elsewhere, by cspell and its custom dictionaries. Grammar and style (word repetition, agreement, punctuation flow) is what this check looks at. Two layers, one goal Spelling and grammar are deliberately split across two checks. That keeps SAP product names you have already allowed in the custom dictionaries from being re-flagged here, and it keeps each check's output focused and easy to read.

The check runs on pull requests that target the dev branch and that touch Markdown prose: Aspect Value File types .md files under docs/ and news/ Trigger Pull requests targeting dev Language en-US only .mdx files Intentionally excluded for now # From .github/workflows/check-grammar.yml patterns: docs/**/*.md news/**/*.md language: en-US Why .mdx is skipped .mdx pages mix Markdown with JSX and import lines. Those lines look like broken sentences to a prose checker and generate the most false positives, so they are left out until the rules are tuned further. Plain .md pages (the vast majority of content, including everything the Quick Start editor produces) are fully covered. LanguageTool scans the tracked docs/ and news/ .md files on each run, and reviewdog then narrows the visible annotations down to the lines you actually changed in the PR. You will not be shown pre-existing issues in parts of a file you never touched.

This is the most important thing to understand as a contributor: the grammar check is non-blocking by design. It can surface warnings, but it can never turn red and it can never stop your pull request from merging. Two independent safeguards guarantee this: The action is run without reviewdog's fail-on-error flag (and exposes no input to turn it on), so reviewdog exits successfully no matter how many findings it reports. The step also carries continue-on-error, so even a hiccup (a read-only token on a fork PR, or the bundled server being slow to boot) cannot make the check fail. The reported level is warning, which only sets the severity label on the comments; it does not change the pass/fail outcome. This one is advisory If you see grammar suggestions, treat them as a helpful second read, not a gate. You are free to apply the ones that improve your text and ignore the ones that do not fit (technical phrasing, intentional style, product terminology).

Where you see the findings depends on how you opened the PR: Your situation Where suggestions show up Branch on the main repository (core contributors) Annotations on the Checks tab, inline on your changed lines (github-pr-check) Pull request from a fork GitHub issues a read-only token, so the Checks-tab annotations cannot be posted. Open the grammar step's Actions run log to see the raw output, and a maintainer can relay any grammar suggestions on the pull request if needed If you contributed through a fork (the recommended path for most community members) and do not see inline annotations, that is expected. Open the workflow run from the Actions tab and read the grammar step's log to see the same suggestions.

To keep the signal clean, several categories and rules are switched off on purpose: Turned off Why TYPOS category Spelling is owned by cspell and the custom dictionaries; this avoids re-flagging allowed SAP terms. TYPOGRAPHY category Curly quotes, fancy dashes, and arrows are noisy against code and Markdown. A set of Markdown-noise rules Rules like whitespace, underscores in words, and bracket pairing misfire on Markdown and code; they are disabled individually. # From .github/workflows/check-grammar.yml disabled_categories: TYPOS,TYPOGRAPHY disabled_rules: WHITESPACE_RULE,EN_QUOTES,DASH_RULE,WORD_CONTAINS_UNDERSCORE,...

Here is the short version of how to work with this check: Read the suggestions, apply what helps. A flagged repeated word or missing comma is usually worth a quick fix. Do not chase a green check. There is nothing to turn green here. The check is informational. Found a false positive? Maintainers tune the check by appending the offending rule id to the disabled_rules list in the workflow. If a legitimate phrasing keeps getting flagged, mention it in your PR and a maintainer can silence that specific rule. warning Because the check only reads .md files, prose inside .mdx pages is not proofread automatically today. Give those pages an extra manual read before you submit.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 20, 2026 by cernus76 The H1 Title check makes sure the title of a page comes from the front matter title: field, not from a level-1 Markdown heading in the body. It is a blocking check: if a changed page contains a # heading, the check fails until it is removed.
documents.s: H1 Title Check for Reference Architectures

documents.t: Every Architecture Center page already declares its title in the front matter: --- title: SAP Event-Driven Architecture Technology --- Docusaurus renders that title: as the page's heading automatically, and also uses it for the browser tab, SEO, and social-media previews (see the front matter guide). If you also add a # heading in the body, the page ends up with two titles, a duplicated <h1> that hurts accessibility and SEO and breaks the document outline. So the rule is simple: The title comes from the front matter title: field. Body headings start at ## (level 2) and go deeper from there (###, ####). A Markdown body must never contain a # (level-1) heading.
documents.s: Why the title lives in the front matter

documents.t: On a pull request that changes Markdown (.md or .mdx) under docs/, the check scans each changed file for a level-1 # heading in the body and fails if it finds one. It is careful to only flag a genuine title heading: The front matter block (between the opening and closing ---) is ignored, so a YAML # comment is never flagged. Fenced code blocks (``` or ~~~) are ignored, so a shell # comment inside a code sample is never flagged. Only a single leading # followed by a space counts. ## and deeper headings, a shebang (#!/usr/bin/env), and a hashtag (#example) are not flagged. info It also triggers when the workflow file itself (.github/workflows/check-h1-title.yml) changes, so maintainers can validate adjustments to the check safely.

Like the spelling and typo checks, this check reports inline on the Files changed tab, pinned to the offending # line, and writes a short summary to the check's job summary. (It is not repeated in the sticky pull request comment.)
documents.s: Where you will see the results

documents.t: Open the flagged page at the line the annotation points to. Delete the # heading line. The title is already set by the front matter title: field, so you do not need a heading for it. If the heading text differs from your front matter title and you want that wording, update the front matter title: instead. Demote any real body headings. If the # was actually a section heading (not the title), change it and its sub-headings down one level so the body starts at ##. Push the fix to the same branch and the check runs again automatically. tip If you contribute through the no-code Quick Start editor, it sets the title in the front matter for you, so you will not hit this check.
