Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 The SAP Architecture Center is a public site, open to everyone on the internet. A link that only works inside the SAP network or behind single sign-on (SSO) is a dead end for external readers. This check scans the Markdown you changed and flags any link that points to an SAP-internal-only host.
documents.s: Internal Link Check for SAP-Only Hosts in Content

documents.t: When your pull request (PR) touches Markdown under docs/ or news/, this workflow looks at the files you added or modified and searches them for links to hosts that are reachable only from inside SAP. It does not scan the whole site, only your changed .md and .mdx files, so it runs fast and points straight at your edits. The goal is simple: everything we publish should work for every visitor. An internal wiki page or an internal tooling link may be perfectly valid for you, but a customer, partner, or community member reading the public site will hit a login wall or a "server not found" error. Where this fits This is one of several content checks that run on every PR. For the big picture and the full list, see the Overview and Operational Workflows pages. For how results are surfaced across all checks, see Errors & Warnings.

The check matches the following internal-only host patterns, case-insensitively, inside any link in your content. Host pattern What it is *.tools.sap Internal tooling (code hosting, project tracking, and similar) *.int.sap Internal services (internal wikis and intranet apps) *.sap.corp Legacy corporate network hosts sap.sharepoint.com Internal SharePoint A couple of details worth knowing: Subdomains count. Any host ending in one of these patterns is flagged, for example a deep subdomain under *.tools.sap or *.sap.corp. Protocol-relative links are caught too. A link that starts with // and omits the https: scheme (for example //<internal-host>/path) is matched as well, not just a full https:// link. Look-alike hosts are safe. The check uses a host-label boundary, so a decoy like a .sapient.com host is not mistaken for a .sap host.

Not every SAP host is internal. The following customer-facing hosts are public and are not flagged, so you can link to them freely: *.cloud.sap *.hana.ondemand.com docs.sap help.sap.com me.sap.com community.sap.com Prefer a public source When you need to point readers at SAP material, use a public destination first, most often help.sap.com or community.sap.com. These are the public homes for official documentation and community content.

If the check finds an internal-only link, it reports in three places so you cannot miss it: An "Internal link"-titled annotation inline on the Files changed tab, attached to the exact line. A Check Internal Links section in the sticky PR comment, which gathers the blocking findings from this and the other content checks. A job summary on the workflow run, listing each hit as path:line:url. A finding here is a blocking error: the check fails until the internal link is gone. The message tells you the file, the line, and the offending URL. note If your PR changes no Markdown under docs/ or news/, the check simply reports that there is nothing to scan and passes.
documents.s: How results appear on your PR

documents.t: You have two options: Replace the internal link with a public equivalent: the same information on a customer-facing host such as help.sap.com or community.sap.com. Remove the link if no public equivalent exists, and reword the sentence so it still reads well. Here is a concrete before/after. The "before" stands in for an internal-only link. The host shown is a non-internal placeholder so this page itself stays clean: <!-- Before: internal-only, breaks for public visitors (placeholder host) --> See the [onboarding guide](https://wiki.corp.example/onboarding) for details. <!-- After: public, works for everyone --> See the [onboarding guide](https://help.sap.com/docs) for details. If the content you were linking to simply has no public counterpart, drop the link and keep the surrounding prose standalone: <!-- After (removal): no public equivalent available --> Follow your team's internal onboarding guide before you start. Even "example" internal URLs are flagged This page is scanned by this very check. It matches any host ending in *.tools.sap, *.int.sap, *.sap.corp, or sap.sharepoint.com when it appears as a link (with https://, http://, or a protocol-relative //), whether the host is real or an invented example, and even inside a code block or inline code, because the scan reads the raw text. A bare mention of such a hostname in prose, with no scheme or //, is not flagged. Labelling a host as a "placeholder" does not exempt it. In examples, use a host that does not end in one of those patterns at all, as the before/after above does.
documents.s: How to fix a flagged link

documents.t: External Links: verifies that your public links actually resolve. Front Matter Properties and SEO Front Matter: validate the metadata at the top of each page. Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 Most pages in this section describe the content checks that run on your pull request and give you line-by-line feedback. This page is different: it tours the operational workflows that build the site, publish it, and keep the supply chain healthy. Unlike the content checks, these workflows run mostly in the background. As a contributor you rarely interact with them directly. The build and deployment workflows run after your change is merged or on a schedule, while the security scans run on a schedule and, for CodeQL and the dependency and workflow audits, on your pull request before merge. They become most relevant to you when your change touches dependencies (package.json, the lockfile) or the workflow files themselves. If that is you, read on. If you are only editing or adding reference-architecture content, you can safely skim. Where these live All of these workflows are defined in the .github/workflows/ directory of the repository. The descriptions below reflect what those files actually do.
documents.s: Build, Deploy, and Security Scanning Workflows

documents.t: Three workflows build the site; two of them also publish it. Workflow File Trigger What it does Build for GitHub Pages build-main.yml Push to main or dev Installs dependencies and builds the site, then uploads the result as a Pages artifact. Deploy to Cloudflare deploy-to-cloudflare.yml Push to main, or manual run The production deployment. Builds with backend configuration and exported diagrams, then publishes to Cloudflare Pages. Deploy to GitHub Pages deploy-manual.yml Manual run only A manual build and publish to GitHub Pages, useful for fork builds and previews.

Whenever a change lands on main or dev, the build-main.yml workflow runs a clean install (npm ci) and a production build (npm run build) on Node.js 24. If the build succeeds, it uploads the compiled site as a Pages artifact. This workflow only verifies that the site still compiles after a merge; it does not publish anything (publishing is handled by the deploy workflows). That is why a broken internal link (Docusaurus fails the build on those by default) or malformed front matter can fail it.

The deploy-to-cloudflare.yml workflow is the one that updates the public production site. It runs when a change reaches main, and can also be started manually. Compared with the plain build, it does extra work so the deployed site is complete: fetches contributor details from the GitHub API, exports the Draw.io diagrams to SVG (and caches them to speed up later runs), builds the site with the backend environment configuration, and rewrites Draw.io links to their hashed URLs. The finished build is then published to Cloudflare Pages. For how diagrams are authored and exported, see the diagramming guide.

The deploy-manual.yml workflow is triggered on demand (workflow_dispatch). It performs the same diagram export and build steps and publishes to GitHub Pages. It is especially useful for fork builds, for example previewing your contribution on your own GitHub Pages site before opening a pull request. You do not deploy by hand As a contributor you never need to run these yourself. Merging an approved change is what moves it toward production. The manual deploy exists mainly for maintainers and for fork previews.

These workflows protect the project from vulnerable dependencies and risky workflow changes. Three run automatically; one is manual. Workflow File Trigger Purpose CodeQL codeql.yml Push and PRs to dev, plus a weekly schedule Static code scanning for JavaScript/TypeScript and GitHub Actions. Scorecard scorecard.yml Push to dev, weekly, and branch-protection changes OpenSSF supply-chain security scoring. Security Audit security-audit.yml PRs touching dependencies or workflows, plus weekly and manual Audits npm scripts, runs npm audit, lints workflows, and reviews dependencies. REUSE compliance reuse-check.yml Manual run only Checks license and copyright compliance.

CodeQL is GitHub's static-analysis engine. The codeql.yml workflow scans the javascript-typescript and actions code on every push and pull request to dev, and again on a weekly schedule. Findings appear in the repository's code-scanning dashboard.

The scorecard.yml workflow runs the OpenSSF Scorecard, which rates the project against a set of supply-chain security best practices (such as pinned dependencies and branch protection). It runs on pushes to dev, weekly, and whenever a branch-protection rule changes.

The security-audit.yml workflow is the one most likely to touch your pull request, but only if your change modifies package.json, package-lock.json, or anything under .github/workflows/. It also runs weekly and can be started manually. It bundles several checks: Audit npm scripts: inspects package.json for dangerous lifecycle hooks (such as preinstall, postinstall, prepare) and suspicious command patterns, and flags scripts that pull in and execute code. npm audit: runs npm audit to surface known vulnerabilities in dependencies and uploads the results to the code-scanning dashboard. On a pull request from a fork the dashboard upload is skipped (the token is read-only), but the audit output and job summary still appear. Audit workflows: lints every workflow with actionlint and checks for risky patterns, for example unpinned third-party actions or missing permission blocks. Dependency Review: on pull requests, uses GitHub's dependency-review action to block newly introduced dependencies that carry high-severity vulnerabilities or disallowed (strong copyleft) licenses. If you add or update a dependency Expect the Security Audit to run on your pull request. If it reports a high-severity vulnerability or a disallowed license, the dependency-review step will fail and the maintainers will ask you to pick a different package or version. This is normal, and it keeps the project's dependency tree clean.

The reuse-check.yml workflow runs the FSFE REUSE tool, which verifies that every file carries clear license and copyright information. It is a manual check (workflow_dispatch), used to verify compliance on demand rather than on every change. Scanners target dev, not main The security scanners (CodeQL and Scorecard) run against the dev branch. The main branch receives only validated content that has already been promoted from dev, so scanning dev is where issues are caught first.

New here? Start with the community intro and the contribution process. Contributing a new reference architecture? The no-code Quick Start editor is the recommended path. Curious about the checks that give you direct feedback on a PR? See the Automated Checks overview and Errors & Warnings.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 When you add an image or a diagram to the SAP Architecture Center, it should actually be used somewhere. The Orphan Files check makes sure of that: it confirms every asset you add is referenced by at least one Markdown page, so unused files do not quietly pile up in the repository. This page explains what the check looks at, how it decides between an error and a warning, where you see the results, and how to fix anything it flags. For the full picture of how the checks fit together, see the Automated Checks overview.
documents.s: Orphan Files Check for Unreferenced Assets

documents.t: The check runs on a pull request only when you add or modify asset files. It does not re-scan the whole repository every time. It targets these locations and file types: What Details Folders watched assets/, diagrams/, and docs/ File types .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .svg, .drawio, .docx Scope Only assets added, modified, or renamed in your PR, compared against the base branch info Because it compares your branch against the base branch, nothing happens if your PR touches no assets. In that case the check reports that there is nothing to review and passes immediately.

For each new or changed asset, the check searches all Markdown files (.md and .mdx) in the repository for a reference to that asset's file name. If a page embeds or links the file, the asset counts as used. There is one important nuance for reference architectures. When an asset lives inside a reference-architecture folder (a path like docs/ref-arch/RA0001/), the reference that "counts" must come from a Markdown page within that same RA directory. This prevents a same-named file in a different RA from accidentally masking a genuine orphan. note Shared assets that live outside any RA#### folder (for example under assets/ or diagrams/) are matched repository-wide: any Markdown page that references them counts.
documents.s: How it decides whether an asset is "used"

documents.t: The check produces one of two signals for a flagged asset: Outcome When Effect Error The asset is referenced nowhere in any Markdown file Blocking: the check fails and the PR cannot merge until it is resolved Warning The asset is referenced only outside its own RA directory Non-blocking: the PR can still merge, but you should verify The warning exists on purpose. An asset matched only outside its own RA directory is usually one of two things: a legitimately shared asset, or a same-named file that happens to match a reference elsewhere while the real file in your RA is actually unused. Rather than block a genuinely shared asset, the check warns so you can confirm which case applies. tip A warning is not a failure. If the asset is intentionally shared, you can leave it as is. If it turns out your RA page never references its own copy, treat the warning as encouragement to add the reference or remove the file.

The findings show up in three places on your pull request: Inline annotations on the Files changed tab, titled Orphan files, marked as an error or a warning on the affected asset. A Check Orphan Files section in the sticky PR comment, aggregated with the other content checks. This section lists blocking errors only. A job summary on the workflow run, listing each flagged asset with a clear status icon. Warnings are not in the sticky comment A non-blocking warning (an asset referenced only outside its own RA folder) appears inline on the Files changed tab and in the job summary, but not in the sticky PR comment. A pull request with only warnings still shows this check as a pass. A clean run simply reports that no unreferenced files were found.

You have two straightforward options whenever an asset is flagged: Reference it: embed or link the asset from the page where it belongs. Remove it: delete the file if you added it by mistake or no longer need it.

Say you add a banner image for a new reference architecture: docs/ref-arch/RA0042/assets/hero.png ...but you forget to actually embed it in the RA page. Because no Markdown page references hero.png, the check reports an error. The inline annotation on the Files changed tab reads: Asset is not referenced in any Markdown file and the job summary lists the offending file: - ❌ docs/ref-arch/RA0042/assets/hero.png To fix it, embed the image in your RA's Markdown page: ![Reference architecture overview](./assets/hero.png) Once a page inside docs/ref-arch/RA0042/ references the file, the check passes. warning If you only reference hero.png from a page in a different RA folder, you will get a warning instead of a pass, because the reference does not live in the asset's own RA directory. Add the reference from within the correct RA to clear it.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 Every reference architecture lives in a readme.md whose front matter carries two linked fields: an id and a slug. This check keeps those fields valid and makes sure no two reference architectures ever claim the same id across the whole site.
documents.s: Reference Architecture ID and Slug Validation Check

documents.t: The id is the stable, permanent identity of a reference architecture, and the slug is the public URL it is served from. The two must agree, and the id must be unique, otherwise two pages would compete for the same address and links would break. This check runs automatically on every pull request so that collisions are caught before they ever reach the live site. The id and slug are generated for you You are not meant to invent these values yourself. The id and its matching slug are assigned by an external application: our no-code Quick Start editor generates a valid id and the correct slug when you scaffold a new reference architecture. These initial values are temporary placeholders: the Architecture Center team finalises them while reviewing your contribution, so the id on the live site may differ from the one you first received. This check is not the generator. It is a safety net that verifies nobody has changed those values by hand or accidentally duplicated an id that another reference architecture already uses. In normal use, if you let the tooling create your pages, the check simply passes. If you want the bigger picture of how all the pull-request checks fit together, start with the Automated Checks overview.

The check validates three things about each reference architecture readme.md: Field Rule id Must be exactly six characters, each one a lowercase letter a–z or a digit 0–9. id Must be unique across every reference architecture on the site. slug Must be exactly /ref-arch/<id>: the same six-character id, prefixed with /ref-arch/. So if your id is a06a95, your slug must be /ref-arch/a06a95. Nothing more, nothing less. Two pages are deliberately skipped The conceptual landing page at docs/ref-arch/readme.md (whose slug is just /ref-arch) and the RA0000 demo page do not follow the /ref-arch/<id> convention, so the check leaves them alone. For the full meaning of id, slug, and the other front matter fields, see the Front Matter guide.

This check is triggered when a pull request touches a docs/ref-arch/**/readme.md file (or the check's own script or workflow). There is an important subtlety in how it decides what passes and what fails: To verify that id values are globally unique, the check reads every reference architecture readme.md in the repository, not only the ones you changed. But only a changed file can actually fail the check. If a problem exists purely in files your pull request never touched, it is not held against you. Duplicate id is a special case A duplicate id involves two files. The check reports it when either of the two colliding files was changed in your pull request, and it points the error at the file you changed, so the fix lands where you are working.
documents.s: What gets checked, and what can fail

documents.t: When something is wrong, the check reports one of four error types: Error Meaning MISSING id The readme.md has no id field in its front matter. INVALID id The id is present but not exactly six characters of a–z / 0–9. SLUG MISMATCH The slug is not exactly /ref-arch/<id> for this file's id. DUPLICATE id Another reference architecture already uses this id.

If the check finds a problem, it surfaces in three places so you cannot miss it: Inline annotations pinned directly to the offending id: or slug: line in your pull request diff (a MISSING id error, having no line to point at, is attached to the file as a whole). A Check Reference Architecture IDs section inside the sticky pull-request comment that aggregates the content checks. A job summary on the check's run, listing every error it found. A passing run simply reports that all files have valid, unique ids.

Seeing one of these errors usually means an id or slug was typed or copied by hand, rather than left as the tooling generated it. The cleanest fix is to use the generator (see the tip below). If you do need to correct the front matter directly, make sure your reference architecture's readme.md has a six-character id and a slug that matches it exactly: --- id: a06a95 slug: /ref-arch/a06a95 title: SAP Event-Driven Architecture Technology # ...other front matter fields... --- Here is what each error is telling you to do: MISSING id: add an id field with a valid six-character value. INVALID id: fix the value so it is exactly six characters, lowercase letters and digits only. For example, A06A95 (uppercase) and a06a9 (five characters) both fail; a06a95 passes. SLUG MISMATCH: set the slug to /ref-arch/<id>, reusing the exact id. If your id is a06a95, the slug is /ref-arch/a06a95. DUPLICATE id: this usually means an id was copied from another page. Regenerate the page with the tooling, or give it a different, unused id (and update its slug to match). Let Quick Start generate the id for you The easiest way to never hit these errors is to not type the id by hand. Our no-code Quick Start editor generates the id and slug for you when you scaffold a new reference architecture. If you start from the create-ref-arch-skeleton template instead, it leaves placeholder values that the Architecture Center team finalises during review, so do not edit them by hand to force this check green.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 Search engines truncate a page title or description that is too long, and gain nothing from one that is too short. This check measures the length of the title and description fields in your front matter on each published docs/ page your pull request changes, so your pages look their best in search results.
documents.s: SEO Front Matter Check for Titles and Descriptions

documents.t: When you open a pull request, this check reads the title and description from the front matter of each affected page and measures how many characters each one has. It then decides whether that length is comfortable, slightly off, or clearly wrong. Pages marked draft: true or unlisted: true are skipped, because search engines do not index them, so their title and description lengths do not matter. info This is a length check only. It does not judge whether your wording is good, nor whether a field is missing from the schema. That is the job of the Front Matter Properties check. Here, an empty or absent title or description is reported as "missing or empty" and fails the build.

Each field has a recommended range (the ideal range for SEO) and wider hard bounds. Staying inside the recommended range keeps the check quiet. Drifting outside it but staying within the hard bounds raises a warning. Going past the hard bounds, or leaving the field empty, fails the build. Field Recommended range Hard bounds (fail outside) title 40–60 characters 20–65 characters description 120–160 characters 50–200 characters

The check produces one of two outcomes per field. Warning (non-blocking): the value is outside the recommended range but still within the hard bounds. For example, a title of 35 characters, or a description of 100. Your build is not blocked, but you are encouraged toward the ideal range. Error (blocking): the value is empty, or outside the hard bounds (way too short or way too long). For example, a title of 72 characters, or a description of 40. This fails the check and blocks the merge until you fix it. note A short section page with a legitimately brief title will warn rather than fail, as long as it stays within the hard bounds. Warnings are safe to leave in place, but they are a good hint that the field is worth polishing.

The check reports in three places, so you do not have to search through raw logs: Inline annotations on the Files changed tab of your pull request, attached to the exact title: or description: line, marked as a warning or an error. A Check SEO Front Matter section in the sticky pull request comment. It lists only the blocking errors (each as a path:line location followed by its message), or a success line when there are none. Non-blocking warnings are not repeated here. They stay as inline annotations. The job summary for the check run, which lists the recommended lengths, the failing bounds, how many pages were checked, and the error and warning counts.
The message tells you the current character count and the range it should fall into. Adjust the wording until the length lands inside the recommended range.

An 82-character title fails with "way too long" because it exceeds the hard maximum of 65: # Fails: 82 characters title: SAP Integration Suite Reference Architecture for Enterprise Event-Driven Messaging Trim it to about 50 characters, inside the recommended 40–60 range: # Passes: 49 characters title: Event-Driven Messaging with SAP Integration Suite
documents.s: A title that is too long

documents.t: A description just below the recommended floor of 120 (but still above the hard minimum of 50) only warns. Expand it toward ~140 characters to clear the warning: # Warns: 88 characters, below the recommended 120 description: A reference architecture for event-driven messaging on SAP Business Technology Platform. # Passes: 137 characters, inside the recommended 120-160 description: A reference architecture for event-driven messaging on SAP Business Technology Platform, covering brokers, topics, and consumer patterns. warning A description of 30 characters is below the hard minimum of 50 and will fail, not warn. Give every published page a real one- or two-sentence description. tip Only the changed docs Markdown on your pull request is checked, that is the pages you added, modified, or renamed under docs/, not the whole site. If your pull request touches no Markdown under docs/, this check has nothing to do and passes immediately.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 When you open a pull request, a spelling check reads the Markdown you changed and flags words it does not recognise. It runs on cspell, a fast, open-source spell checker built for code and documentation.
documents.s: Spelling Check with cspell for Docs and News Pages

documents.t: cspell looks at the prose in your .md and .mdx files and compares every word against its dictionaries. Anything it cannot find is reported as an unknown word. The goal is simple: catch typos in reference architectures and news before they reach readers, while leaving the many legitimate technical terms we use every day alone. Why a spell checker needs help Our content is full of product names, acronyms, and partner and author names that no general English dictionary knows. cspell handles those through custom dictionaries, so a flagged word is often a real typo, not a false alarm.

The check is incremental: it only looks at Markdown that was added or modified compared to the base branch of your pull request. Pages you did not touch are never scanned, so historical gaps in older content can never block your contribution. Aspect Value Trigger Pull requests targeting dev or main Scope Files added, modified, or renamed vs. the PR base File types .md and .mdx under docs/ and news/ Also triggers on Changes to cspell.json, .cspell/**, or the workflow file itself Runtime Node.js 24, cspell 9.1.0 In short: if your pull request changes a Markdown page under docs/ or news/, or touches the spelling configuration, this check runs against just those changed files. A pull request that changes only the spelling configuration, with no Markdown, has nothing to re-check and passes automatically; the configuration simply takes effect the next time a page that relies on it changes.

If cspell finds even one unknown word in your changed files, the check fails. A failing check marks the pull request so maintainers know something needs attention before merging. This is a prompt, not a punishment A failed spelling check almost always means one of two things: a genuine typo you can fix in seconds, or a real term that simply needs to be added to a dictionary. Both are quick.

The findings show up in two places: Inline annotations on the Files changed tab. Each unknown word is pinned to its exact line and column, under the annotation title Spelling. The message follows this format: docs/ref-arch/my-architecture/readme.md:42:17 - Unknown word (Kubernets) The job summary. The check run also lists every finding in its summary, wrapped in a code block, so you can scan them all in one place. No sticky comment Spelling findings are intentionally not posted into the single sticky pull request comment that aggregates other checks. Keeping dozens of word-level notes out of that comment keeps it readable. The inline annotations and the job summary are where you review spelling.
You have two good options, depending on whether the flagged word is wrong or simply unknown.

Fix the spelling in your Markdown and push again. The check re-runs automatically. <!-- before --> We deploy the workload to a Kubernets cluster. <!-- after --> We deploy the workload to a Kubernetes cluster.
documents.s: 1. It is a typo, so correct it

documents.t: Product names, acronyms, partner names, and people's names are correct even though a general dictionary rejects them. Add them to the right custom dictionary so cspell (and everyone's future PRs) accept them. See Custom Dictionaries for which file to use (sap, industry, partners, or people) and how to add a word. Add real words only Only add a word to a dictionary when it is genuinely correct. Adding a misspelling silences the checker for everyone and lets the typo spread.
documents.s: 2. It is a real term, so add it to a dictionary

documents.t: A cspell.json file at the repository root defines the behaviour. A few parts of that configuration explain why some text is never flagged. Configuration highlights Languages: English in three flavours (en, en-US, and en-GB), so both "color" and "colour" are accepted. URLs and e-mail addresses are ignored, so links and contact addresses never trip the checker. Front matter is partly skipped: tags, contributors, author, id, and slug values are ignored via patterns, because those hold slugs and names rather than prose. Ignored paths: some files are never scanned at all: the docs/ref-arch/RA0000/** template, the cookie-and-privacy pages (docs/community/99-cookie-and-privacy/**), the team page (docs/community/10-the-team.md), plus images (.png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif), .svg, and .drawio files. Everything else (the body of your page, including headings and list items) is fair game for the spell checker.

Spelling is one of three complementary checks on your prose. They overlap a little but each catches different things: Check Catches Blocks the PR? Spelling (this page) Unknown words vs. the dictionaries Yes Typos Common misspellings and typo patterns see that page Grammar Grammar and style issues see that page Think of spelling as the first line of defence for individual words, with Typos and Grammar adding broader checks on top.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 15, 2026 by cernus76 The Typos check scans the Markdown you changed for common, high-confidence misspellings: the kind of slip that no reader should have to stumble over. It is deliberately narrow: it only reacts to words that look like a known typo, so it rarely gets in the way of valid SAP, industry, or partner terminology.
documents.s: Typos Check for Common Misspellings in Markdown

documents.t: When your pull request touches Markdown under docs/ or news/, this check runs the typos binary (pinned to version 1.50.3) over the files you added or modified. If it finds a likely misspelling, it flags it and the check fails. Because it is scoped to changed files only, it never flags pre-existing typos elsewhere in the project. You are responsible for the lines you touched, and nothing more. The check is triggered by changes to any of these paths: Path What it covers docs/**/*.md, docs/**/*.mdx Reference architectures and community docs news/**/*.md, news/**/*.mdx News articles _typos.toml The check's own configuration .github/workflows/check-typos.yml The workflow definition

This is the single most important thing to understand about Typos, especially if you have already met the Spelling check (cspell). The key difference typos only flags words that closely resemble a known misspelling: for example recieve → receive, or teh → the. It does not flag a word simply because the word is unfamiliar. That means an unusual-but-correct product name, acronym, or technical term (the kind of word that cspell might not recognise) will almost always pass straight through Typos untouched. There is no need to register SAP product names, partner names, or industry jargon here just because they are uncommon. Think of it this way: Check Reacts to Typical fix Typos (this page) Words that look like a known misspelling Correct the spelling, or allow a wrongly corrected real term Spelling (cspell) Words that are unknown to its dictionaries Add the valid term to a custom dictionary
documents.s: How it differs from the spelling check

documents.t: If Typos finds something, it does three things: Fails the check, which blocks the pull request until it is resolved. Adds inline annotations on the Files changed tab of your PR, right on the offending line. These annotations carry the title "Typos". Writes a job summary listing every typo it found. Not in the PR comment Unlike some other checks, Typos does not post into the sticky summary comment on your PR. Look for its findings as inline annotations on the Files changed tab, or open the check's job summary.
The check reads its rules from _typos.toml at the repository root. Here are the parts worth knowing about.

[default] locale = "en" The en locale is variant-neutral: both en-US and en-GB spellings are accepted, so you will not be pushed from colour to color or vice versa. (typos supports a single locale value, and en is the neutral one.)

Occasionally typos will "correct" a word that is actually valid in our context. To stop that, you map the word to itself under [default.extend-words]. Keys are lowercase. [default.extend-words] advices = "advices" # "remittance advices", a valid accounting term rto = "rto" # Recovery Time Objective alo = "alo" # At-Least-Once (delivery QoS) aks = "aks" # Azure Kubernetes Service aci = "aci" # Azure Container Instance Keep this list small and reactive Only add an entry when typos wrongly corrects a real term. There is no need to pre-register valid vocabulary here. That proactive, exhaustive job belongs to the custom dictionaries used by the spelling check.
[default.extend-identifiers] The extend-identifiers section is for identifier-like tokens (code symbols or names) that typos should never touch. It is currently empty.

[files] extend-exclude = [ "*.min.js", "*.lock", "*.svg", "*.drawio", "docs/ref-arch/RA0000/", "docs/community/02-Guidelines/08-Automated-Checks/01-check-spelling.md", "docs/community/02-Guidelines/08-Automated-Checks/02-dictionaries.md", "docs/community/02-Guidelines/08-Automated-Checks/03-check-typos.md", "docs/community/02-Guidelines/08-Automated-Checks/13-pr-checks-errors-and-warnings.md", ] Pattern Why it is excluded *.min.js Minified JavaScript, not prose *.lock Dependency lock files *.svg Vector graphics markup *.drawio Draw.io diagram source (see the Draw.io Files check and the diagramming guide) docs/ref-arch/RA0000/ The new-RA template, which holds Latin lorem-ipsum placeholder text The Automated Checks pages that show example misspellings (including this one) They must display real misspellings such as recieve and teh as examples. typos has no per-line ignore, so the whole file is excluded here. cspell still scans these pages, with a scoped cspell:ignore for just the example words
You have two paths, depending on who is right: you or the tool.
documents.s: How to fix a reported typo

documents.t: Correct the spelling in your Markdown and push again. The inline annotation tells you the exact file, line, and suggested correction. docs/ref-arch/my-architecture/index.md:42:8: error: `recieve` should be `receive` Change recieve to receive, commit, and the check turns green.

If typos is flagging a word that is genuinely correct in our content, add it to extend-words in _typos.toml, mapping it to itself. For example, suppose a page legitimately uses the accounting term remittance advices and typos tries to "fix" advices. The allowance looks like this: [default.extend-words] advices = "advices" # "remittance advices", a valid accounting term Choose the right list Add a word to _typos.toml only when typos is actively wrongly correcting it. If instead the Spelling check reports a word as unknown, that word belongs in a custom dictionary, not here. The two lists solve different problems.
documents.s: 2. It is a valid term being wrongly corrected

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 8, 2026 by cernus76 SAP adopts the Contributor Covenant 2.1 across our open source projects to ensure a welcoming and open culture for everyone involved.
documents.s: SAP Open Source Code of Conduct (Contributor Covenant)

documents.t: We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in our community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience, education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race, caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation. We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming, diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our community include: Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes, and learning from the experience Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall community Examples of unacceptable behavior include: The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances of any kind Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks Public or private harassment Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address, without their explicit permission Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a professional setting

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive, or harmful. Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for moderation decisions when appropriate.

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address, posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be reported to the community leaders responsible for enforcement at ospo@sap.com (SAP Open Source Program Office). All complaints will be reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly. All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the reporter of any incident.
Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

Community Impact: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed unprofessional or unwelcome in the community. Consequence: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

Community Impact: A violation through a single incident or series of actions. Consequence: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent ban.

Community Impact: A serious violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior. Consequence: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period. Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

Community Impact: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals. Consequence: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the community.

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1, available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html. Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder. For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq. Translations are available at https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations.

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 8, 2026 by cernus76 Two components have been developed for the Architecture Center: The Contributors component: This section displays a list of contributors in an admonition at the bottom of the main page of the reference architecture, acknowledging their efforts and input. The draw.io component: This section features an admonition for a Draw.io file located in the architecture section of the page. Users can either download the file for offline use or create an online copy to edit directly. You can define a specific title for your draw.io file. By default, the page title will be used.

documents.s: How to Contribute to SAP Architecture Center

documents.t: You are welcome to contribute content (code, documentation etc.) to this open source project. There are some important things to know: You must comply to the license of this project, accept the Developer Certificate of Origin (see below) before being able to contribute. The acknowledgement to the DCO will usually be requested from you as part of your first pull request to this project. Please adhere to our Code of Conduct. If you plan to use generative AI for your contribution, please see our guideline below. Not all proposed contributions can be accepted. Some features may fit another project better or doesn't fit the general direction of this project. Of course, this doesn't apply to most bug fixes, but a major feature implementation for instance needs to be discussed with one of the maintainers first. Possibly, one who touched the related code or module recently. The more effort you invest, the better you should clarify in advance whether the contribution will match the project's direction. The best way would be to just open an issue to discuss the feature you plan to implement (make it clear that you intend to contribute). We will then forward the proposal to the respective code owner. This avoids disappointment.

Contributors will be asked to accept a DCO before they submit the first pull request to this project, this happens in an automated fashion during the submission process. SAP uses the standard DCO text of the Linux Foundation.

As artificial intelligence evolves, AI-generated code is becoming valuable for many software projects, including open-source initiatives. While we recognize the potential benefits of incorporating AI-generated content into our open-source projects there are certain requirements that need to be reflected and adhered to when making contributions. Please see our guideline for AI-generated code contributions to SAP Open Source Software Projects for these requirements.

Make sure the change is welcome (see General Remarks). Choose your preferred contribution method: Get Started with Quick Start: a no-code approach. Contribute with AI Agents: use an AI coding agent with the repository's AGENTS.md context. Contribute manually: fork the repository, create a feature or update branch, and make your changes with your preferred tools. Please note that the previous command-line scaffolding tool is no longer available. Before creating a pull request, sync your forked repository with the main repository to incorporate the latest changes and avoid merge conflicts. (Not needed for the Quick Start path, which forks and syncs for you.) Create a pull request (PR) in the repository using your feature or update branch. Note If your contribution was created using Quick Start, this step is handled automatically, so no manual PR creation is needed. Follow the link posted by the CLA assistant to your pull request and accept it, as described above. Wait for our code review and approval, possibly enhancing your change on request. Note Note that the maintainers have many duties. So, depending on the required effort for reviewing, testing, and clarification, this may take a while. Once the change has been approved and merged, we will inform you in a comment. The following diagram shows the overall lifecycle of contributor changes in the SAP Architecture Center repository Best Practice Regularly sync with the main repository before contributing or creating a pull request to avoid merge conflicts.

To ensure consistent code and documentation formatting across all contributions, we use Prettier for automatic code formatting. Additionally, we provide a .editorconfig file to standardize basic editor settings (such as indentation and line endings) across different IDEs. Please make sure your editor respects these settings for a smooth collaboration experience.

Hosting on Cloudflare The SAP Architecture Center (this site) is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. For information about cookies used by Cloudflare, please refer to Cloudflare’s cookie policy: Cloudflare Cookie Policy.
documents.s: Important information regarding the Privacy Statement

documents.t: This Cookie Statement was updated on 21-Oct-2026. This Cookie Statement describes how SAP (hereinafter also “We”, “Our”) uses cookies and similar technologies to collect and store information when you visit SAP Architecture Center. SAP’s Privacy Statement applies in addition to this Cookie Statement. SAP’s Privacy Statement informs you about the way SAP uses, stores and protects personal data collected. It also informs you of your data protection rights and how to exercise them. We recommend that you read SAP’s Privacy Statement: SAP Architecture Center Privacy Statement.

Cookies are small files placed on your device (computer, tablet or smartphone). When you access a website, a cookie is placed on your device and it will send information to the party that placed the cookie. There are other technologies performing a similar function to cookies. These include inter alia web beacons, clear gifs, and social plug-ins. These are often used in conjunction with cookies to help a website owner understand its users better.
documents.s: What are Cookies and similar technologies?

documents.t: SAP’s websites contain first party Cookies. First party cookies are cookies that are specific to the website that created them. These cookies enable SAP to operate an efficient service and to track patterns of user behavior to SAP’s website.

The difference between a first party cookie and a third party cookie relates to who places the cookie on your device. SAP sometimes allows third parties to place Cookies on your device. Third party cookies are placed on your device by a third party (i.e., not by SAP). While SAP allows third parties to access SAP’s website to place a third-party cookie on your device, SAP does not retain control over the information supplied by the cookies, nor does SAP retain access to this information. This information is controlled wholly by that third party according to the respective privacy policy of the third party. For more information about these Cookies, please click the “Cookie Preferences” link in the footer of the webpage.

Cloudflare, which hosts and delivers this site, may set strictly necessary security cookies on the domain of SAP Architecture Center, such as __cf_bm (bot management) and cf_clearance. These cookies help protect the site against malicious traffic and ensure it loads correctly and securely. Because they are set on our own domain, they behave as first party cookies, and because they are strictly necessary for the security and delivery of the site, they are treated as Required Cookies. For more information, please refer to Cloudflare’s cookie policy: Cloudflare Cookie Policy.
documents.s: What cookies does our hosting provider set?

documents.t: In the United States SAP routinely works with third party analytics and digital marketing providers who facilitate and support SAP (and partner) marketing activities including targeted communications. These activities may involve the sharing of limited Personal Information (personal identifiers and contact information, your interests and interactions with SAP, professional/employment information) for those specific business purposes. In addition to the above, SAP may also share your personal data with other third parties, or for other business purposes, with your explicit consent. SAP endeavors to recognize common opt-out preference signals at a browser level, and frictionlessly exclude you from marketing cookies and associated tracking.
documents.s: Analytics and Digital Marketing in the United States of America

documents.t: SAP wants you to be in a position to make an informed decision for or against the use of cookies which are not strictly necessary for technical features on SAP Architecture Center. If you elect to reject cookies used for advertising, you will be shown advertising that is less targeted to your interests. This will still allow you to use all of the functionality of SAP Architecture Center. When tracking and evaluating the usage behavior of users of the Web Presence by means of cookies or similar technologies includes the processing of your personal data, SAP conducts the processing based on the following legal permissions: GDPR Article 6.I (a) if it is necessary that We ask you for your consent to process your personal data, GDPR Article 6.I (b) if necessary to fulfill (pre-)contractual obligations with you, GDPR Article 6.I (f) if necessary to fulfill (pre-)contractual obligations with the company or other legal body you represent as a customer contact (legitimate interest to efficiently perform or manage SAP’s business operation), or equivalent legal permissions under other relevant national laws, when applicable. SAP differentiates between Required Cookies that are absolutely necessary to enable technical core functionalities, Functional Cookies that allow SAP to analyze the site usage, and Advertising Cookies that are used to serve ads relevant to your interests.

SAP provides you with the option to adjust your preferences for Functional and Advertising Cookies when such cookies are placed on your device. In such a case, you can access preferences at any time by clicking on the “Cookie Statement” link in the footer of the SAP Architecture Center. You can also block and delete cookies by changing your browser settings. To manage cookies using your browser settings, most browsers allow you to refuse or accept all cookies or only to accept certain types of cookies. The process for the management and deletion of cookies can be found in the help function integrated in your browser. If you wish to limit the use of cookies, you may not be able to use all the interactive functions.
documents.s: How can you manage and delete Cookies?

documents.t: Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 8, 2026 by cernus76 A well-structured CSS approach is essential for maintainable, scalable, and performant web applications. Our project leverages global styles, CSS Modules, and CSS custom properties for: Consistency: Shared variables and resets keep the look and feel unified. Isolation: CSS Modules prevent style conflicts between components. Responsiveness: Media queries and flexible layouts adapt to all devices. Performance: Optimized images and layout techniques minimize layout shifts and improve load times. These guidelines help us deliver a robust user experience and make ongoing development easier. As a contributor of reference architecture content, you might not need to worry about this at all. Markdown is styled automatically and we handle the majority of this customization at the site level. Our development team uses these guidelines to provide the rich content on our main page. If you ever contribute a custom component or other site-level modification to our project, the following sections are for you!
documents.s: Design and Styling Guidelines for Contributors

documents.t: Responsive design is critical for the SAP Architecture Center because our users access complex technical content from various devices - from mobile phones during commutes to large desktop monitors in development environments. Our architecture diagrams, code examples, and reference materials must remain readable and functional across all screen sizes. This is achieved using flexible layouts, relative units, and media queries that adapt our content presentation to each device's capabilities. See MDN Responsive Design for a comprehensive guide. The impact on our site is surfaced in our core web vitals score, which influences where pages are ranked for Google searches. Two critical topics are: Minimizing Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) CLS measures unexpected layout shifts during page load. To minimize CLS: Always set width and height attributes on images. Reserve space for dynamic or late-loading content (e.g., ads, embeds). Avoid inserting new content above existing content without user interaction. Use CSS aspect-ratio or min-height for placeholders. See web.dev Optimize CLS for more details. Optimizing Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and Images LCP is a key web performance metric that measures when the largest content element (often a hero image or heading) becomes visible. To optimize LCP: Use modern image formats like WebP for better compression and faster loads. We convert hero and banner images to WebP (see squoosh.app for easy conversion). Use the srcSet and sizes attributes on tags to serve responsive images based on device size and resolution. For example: Always specify width and height to reserve space and reduce layout shift. Use loading="eager" and fetchPriority="high" for above-the-fold images.

Global styles: Located in src/css/custom.css. These apply site-wide and include CSS custom properties (variables), typography, layout resets, and Infima/Docusaurus overrides. CSS Modules: Used for component or page-level styles (e.g., src/components/ReactCarousel/ReactCarousel.module.css, src/theme/DocCard/styles.module.css). These provide local scoping and prevent style conflicts. CSS Custom Properties: Centralized design tokens for spacing, colors, shadows, border-radius, and breakpoints, defined in src/css/custom.css (e.g. var(--spacing-md), var(--shadow-card), var(--border-radius-lg)). Use these instead of hard-coded values. Media queries: Always placed at the bottom of each CSS or CSS module file, grouped together for clarity and maintainability.

Use CSS Custom Properties for consistent spacing, colors, shadows, and dimensions across components. Reference variables like var(--spacing-md) instead of hard-coded values. Prefer CSS Modules for component/page-specific styles. This keeps styles modular and avoids global namespace pollution. Reuse CSS custom properties for common patterns, e.g. spacing (var(--spacing-md)), shadows (var(--shadow-card)), and border radius (var(--border-radius-lg)), instead of redefining values per component. Avoid inline styles completely; use CSS modules or CSS custom properties instead. Keep media queries together at the end of each file to simplify responsive maintenance. Name classes descriptively and use Block Element Modifier (BEM) or similar conventions for clarity. BEM is a naming convention for classes in HTML and CSS that helps keep CSS more maintainable and scalable. Test changes across breakpoints to ensure responsive behavior.

Important: CSS variables do not work in media queries within CSS Modules (.module.css files). This is a technical limitation of CSS Modules processing. ✅ This works in CSS Modules: .myComponent { padding: var(--spacing-md); /* ✅ Works fine */ color: var(--color-primary); /* ✅ Works fine */ } ❌ This does NOT work in CSS Modules: @media (max-width: var(--breakpoint-tablet)) { /* ❌ Variable not resolved */ .myComponent { /* Styles won't apply correctly */ } } ✅ Workaround - Use hardcoded breakpoints in CSS Modules: @media (max-width: 996px) { /* ✅ Use hardcoded values */ .myComponent { /* Styles work correctly */ } }
documents.s: ⚠️ CSS Modules Limitation: Media Query Variables

documents.t: We use CSS custom properties (variables) to maintain consistency and reduce code duplication. Instead of hard-coding values like padding: 16px or border-radius: 20px, use our standardized variables.

Most Common: Spacing: var(--spacing-sm) (8px), var(--spacing-md) (16px), var(--spacing-lg) (24px) Shadows: var(--shadow-card), var(--shadow-card-hover) Border radius: var(--border-radius-md) (12px), var(--border-radius-lg) (20px) Layout: var(--card-max-width) (430px), var(--card-max-width-tablet) (600px) Carousel Specific: Padding: Use the cardClassName prop on the ReactCarousel component to apply consistent padding. The paddedCardContainer class in ReactCarousel.module.css is a good default. Example Usage: .myCard { padding: var(--spacing-md); border-radius: var(--border-radius-lg); box-shadow: var(--shadow-card); } See src/css/custom.css for the complete list of available design tokens (CSS custom properties).

These practices directly improve our site's performance and user experience: Faster loading: CSS variables reduce bundle size by ~25%, meaning faster page loads for users accessing architecture diagrams and documentation Consistent experience: Standardized spacing and shadows ensure our reference architectures and code examples look professional across all devices Easier maintenance: When we need to update our design system (like adjusting card shadows or spacing), we change one variable instead of hunting through dozens of files Below are several examples that demonstrate best practices for improving code styling and overall coding quality.

Suppose you want to increase the left and/or top padding of the hero banner text on the landing page: Locate the relevant CSS class in src/css/custom.css (for global) or the appropriate CSS module if the style is component-specific. Edit the padding property. For example, to increase left padding for .welcome (which wraps the hero text): .welcome { /* ...existing code... */ padding-left: 4rem; /* Increase as needed */ padding-top: 5rem; /* Add or adjust as needed */ /* ...existing code... */ } If the change should only apply at certain breakpoints, add or adjust the relevant media query at the bottom of the file: @media (max-width: 600px) { .welcome { padding-left: 2rem; padding-top: 2rem; } }

Flexbox is widely used in our CSS for layout. For example, the footer and card layouts use flex properties to control direction, alignment, and spacing. Changing Flex Direction for Responsive Footer In src/css/custom.css, the footer links are displayed in a row by default, but switch to a column layout on tablet screens (996px and below): .footer__links { display: flex; justify-content: center !important; align-items: flex-start; width: 100%; margin: 0 auto; } @media (max-width: 996px) { .footer__links { display: flex !important; flex-direction: column !important; align-items: center !important; justify-content: center !important; width: 100%; margin: 0 auto; } } How to change: To switch a flex container from row to column at a breakpoint, add or update the flex-direction property inside the relevant media query. Use align-items and justify-content to control alignment in the new direction. Example: Adjusting Card Layout for Responsiveness In src/components/ReactCarousel/ReactCarousel.module.css, the .cardContainer class changes its max-width and padding at different breakpoints: .cardContainer { padding: 0 var(--spacing-md); box-sizing: border-box; min-height: 320px; max-width: var(--card-max-width); width: 100%; } @media (max-width: 996px) { .cardContainer { max-width: 600px; width: 100%; margin: 0 auto; padding-left: 0; padding-right: 0; display: flex !important; flex-direction: column; } } @media (max-width: 600px) { .cardContainer { min-height: 340px; padding: 0 2px; } } This ensures cards are wider and more readable on tablets, and have minimal padding on mobile.

In src/theme/DocCard/styles.module.css, the .docCard class uses flexbox to stack content vertically and align it to the bottom: .docCard { /* ...existing code... */ display: flex; flex-direction: column; justify-content: flex-end; } display: flex; enables flexbox layout. flex-direction: column; stacks children vertically. justify-content: flex-end; aligns children to the bottom of the card. To change the alignment (e.g., to top or center), adjust justify-content: .docCard { /* ...existing code... */ justify-content: flex-start; /* or center */ }
To change the spacing between tags in a card, edit the gap property in the .tagsRow class: .tagsRow { /* ...existing code... */ gap: 3px; /* Increase for more space between tags */ }

Docusaurus supports global CSS, CSS Modules, and (experimental) CSS-in-JS. See Docusaurus Styling & Layout. For React best practices, see Best Practices for Styling in React and CSS Matters: An Overview of Different CSS Approaches.
MDN: Responsive Design web.dev: Optimize CLS Docusaurus: Styling and Layout React Styling Best Practices CSS Approaches Overview BEM Introduction WebP Image Format Squoosh Image Converter

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 8, 2026 by cernus76 Welcome to the development section of our open source project! Here, we warmly invite everyone, regardless of experience or background, to join us in shaping and improving this project. Contributing is welcoming and rewarding, whether you are adding code, fixing bugs, improving documentation, sharing ideas, or helping with non-technical tasks. We try to provide you with clear guidelines, best practices, and examples to help you get started smoothly and make meaningful contributions that align with our project’s goals and standards. Together, we build a respectful, inclusive, and collaborative environment where every contribution counts.

documents.t: Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 8, 2026 by cernus76 This guide provides best practices for creating and contributing diagrams to the SAP Architecture Center. It covers Draw.io diagrams for SAP solution architectures and Mermaid diagrams for flow-based visualizations. Follow these guidelines to ensure your diagrams are consistent, visually appealing, and easy to understand.
documents.s: Draw.io and Mermaid Diagram Best Practices for SAP

documents.t: Use Draw.io diagrams when: Representing SAP BTP services, cloud products, or technical landscapes. Creating high-level solution architectures that include SAP services, environments, and their interdependencies. Following the SAP BTP Solution Diagram Guidelines to ensure consistency and adherence to SAP design principles.

Use the SAP BTP Starter Kit: Download the SAP BTP Solution Diagram Starter Kit for official icons, templates, and design elements. The starter kit includes pre-configured libraries, reusable templates, and examples to help you get started quickly. Leverage Shape Libraries and Editable Presets: Access the Draw.io Shape Libraries for foundational icons, integration suite icons, and more. Use the Shape Libraries and Editable Presets to explore reusable templates for common SAP BTP scenarios, such as: SAP Build Work Zone (L2) SAP Private Link Service (L2) SAP Cloud Identity Services - Authentication (L2) Maintain Consistency: Level 1 (L1) diagrams: Provide a high-level overview of solution architectures, focusing on key components and their relationships. Level 2 (L2) diagrams: Offer detailed technical representations, including service interactions, data flows, and integration points. Use the same icon sizes, line styles, and text formatting across all diagrams. Avoid creating custom arrows; use the ones provided in the starter kit. Optimize for Readability: Use Level 1 or Level 2 diagrams for detailed technical representations. Follow Repository Structure: Place .drawio files in the drawio/ folder and refer to them in your markdown as in the Components reference. Example structure: ref-arch/ ├─ RAXXXX/ │ ├─ drawio/ │ │ ├─ solution-diagram-1.drawio
SAP BTP Solution Diagram Guidelines YouTube: Mastering Solution Diagrams SAP Solution Diagrams on Lucid Marketplace

Use Mermaid diagrams when: Representing process flows, decision trees, or data workflows. Visualizing non-product-specific flows or abstract concepts. Creating lightweight diagrams directly in markdown files. Note Mermaid-generated svg is automatically optimized for static websites. It is typically 10x-100x smaller than Drawio-generated svg. If you're trying to represent a simple flow, use Mermaid.

Check the code behind these examples by reviewing the underlying markdown, using the edit button at the top of this page. The rendered versions are displayed below for illustrative purposes. Choose the Right Diagram Type: Use flowcharts for processes and workflows. Use sequence diagrams for interactions between components. Use Styling for Consistency: Apply classDef to define consistent styles for nodes and edges. Example: Keep Layouts Intuitive: Use subgraph to group related nodes and reduce clutter. Example: Optimize for the Architecture Center: Use smaller fonts and reduced stroke widths to ensure diagrams render well in the deployed site. Example: Annotate Reverse Flows: Use dashed lines (-.->) for reverse flows and add labels for clarity. Example:

Community of Practice Last updated on Oct 20, 2026 by cernus76 Front Matter plays a crucial role in reference architectures. It defines key aspects such as SEO details, along with essential technical information like the slug (URL), sidebar position, and the date of the last update.
documents.s: Front Matter Fields for Reference Architectures

documents.t: Here is an example of what a page front matter looks like: --- id: a06a95 slug: /ref-arch/a06a95 sidebar_position: 1 title: SAP Event-Driven Architecture Technology description: Please add a description (max 300 characters) keywords: - sap sidebar_label: SAP Event-Driven Architecture Technology image: img/ac-soc-med.png tags: - ref-arch hide_table_of_contents: false hide_title: false toc_min_heading_level: 2 toc_max_heading_level: 4 draft: false unlisted: false contributors: - cernus76 - jmsrpp last_update: author: cernus76 date: 2026-04-21 discussion: github:195 ---
The front matter starts and ends with ---.

Each page receives an id. This id is structured as the following: a06a95 for both the id and will be also reused for the slug. Let's take the following example: id: a06a95. Example: id: a06a95 Do Not Modify This information is auto-assigned during the technical validation.

Each page receives a slug which is used to create the document's URL. This slug is structured as the following: /ref-arch/ is followed by a short UUID XXXXXX /ref-arch/XXXXXX is unique for each document. slug and id are always identical for the Reference Architectures. Example: slug: /ref-arch/a06a95 Do Not Modify This information is auto-assigned during the technical validation.
sidebar_position is used to position the reference architecture on the sidebar. Example: sidebar_position: 1 Do Not Modify This information is auto-assigned during the technical validation.

title defines the page name, the one which will be displayed in the browser tab. title is used for the SEO (used as page title when indexed by the search engines) or when the page is shared on social media. title is also what Docusaurus renders as the page heading, so the title comes from here, not from a heading in the body. It should be clear and concise. Example: title: SAP Event-Driven Architecture Technology Best practice Your title should not be longer than 60 characters. Do not use a # heading for the title Because the title is taken from the title: field above, your Markdown body must not contain a level-1 # heading, it would produce a second, duplicate page title. Start your body headings at ## (level 2) and go deeper from there. This is enforced by the H1 Title check, which fails the pull request if a # heading is found.

description is used for the SEO (used as page description when indexed by the search engines) or when the page is shared on social media. Example: description: Event-driven Architecture(EDA) is a software design pattern for building and integrating systems which focuses on flow of events and resulting reaction triggered by these events. Best practice We recommend to make sure the important part of your description is within the first 110 characters.
keywords is used for specific keywords to find the page. All pages should have sap as default. Example: keywords: - sap - analytics - sac

sidebar_label is the displayed entry on the sidebar. It can be identical to the title or different. It is up to you. It should be clear and concise. Example: sidebar_label: SAP Event-Driven Architecture Technology Best practice Your sidebar label should not be longer than 50 characters.

image is the image which will be displayed when sharing the page. The default image is the SAP Architecture Center image image: img/ac-soc-med.png Example: image: img/ac-soc-med.png Best practice The optimal size should be 1200 x 630.

tags are displayed at the bottom of the page. The tags are defined in a yaml file named tags.yml. It is possible to enrich the file and add new tags. Example: tags: - ref-arch - aws - azure Example of a tag declaration in the tags.yml file: ref-arch: label: "Reference Architecture" description: "Reference Architectures offer standardized, reusable templates for software architecture, providing best practices, guidelines, and blueprints to streamline design, development, and deployment."

hide_table_of_contents allows you to reclaim the space allocated to the Table Of Content (TOC) on the right hand side of the page. In some cases it makes sense to hide the TOC as there is no real use for it. Default value is set to false. Example: hide_table_of_contents: false

hide_title allows you to not display the title of the page on the page. In some cases it makes sense to hide the Title if there is no need for it. Default value is set to false. Example: hide_title: false
toc_min_heading_level allows you to define the minimum level for the TOC. Default value is set to 2. Example: toc_min_heading_level: 2
toc_max_heading_level allows you to define the maximum level for the TOC. Default value is set to 4. Example: toc_max_heading_level: 4

draft defines the status of your page. If it is in draft mode, it means the page is not ready yet. The default value is false If you set this to true, the page will not be part of the build and will not be deployed. If you set this to false, the page will be part of the build and will be deployed. Example: draft: false Best practice Keep the value to true until you are done and ready to submit the page for review.

unlisted defines if your page is visible in the Architecture Center. If it is unlisted, it means the page is deployed and accessible but it is not visible. The default value is false If you set this to true, the page will be part of the build, will be deployed, but will not be visible in the sidebar. You need to access it directly via the defined slug. If you set this to false, the page will be part of the build, will be deployed, and will be visible in the sidebar. Example: unlisted: false Best practice Set the value to true when you want to share the page to a limited number of people for validation.

contributors defines the main contributors of the page. Enter the GitHub username(s). The contributors are displayed at the bottom of the page. Example: contributors: - cernus76 - jmsrpp - navyakhurana Best practice Check the generated admonition to make sure there are no typos in the GitHub usernames.

last_update defines the last update of the page (author + date). The author and date are displayed at the bottom of the page. The date should be YYYY-MM-DD. Example: last_update: author: jmsrpp date: 2026-04-21 Best practice Enter only one author.

discussion links the page to a related discussion thread. If defined on a page with at least one contributors entry, a button is added at the bottom of the page to jump to the matching discussion. Expected format: github:<DISCUSSION-ID> or community:<DISCUSSION-PATH>. Leave it empty if the page has no associated discussion. Example: discussion: github:195

sidebar_custom_props (with a nested category_index) was previously used to list a page in an additional sidebar, such as the SAP ViewPoints. This field is deprecated and will be removed. Do not add it to new pages. You may still see it in older templates (for example docs/ref-arch/RA0000/readme.md); leave existing entries as-is unless you are intentionally cleaning them up. Community of Practice Agents Last updated on Oct 8, 2026 by cernus76 AI (coding) agents have become an integral part of how the community works with the SAP Architecture Center, from writing code that changes the look and feel of the site to putting the final touches on reference architecture content. The repository comes with an AGENTS.md file that provides agents with project context, conventions, and predefined skills located under .agents/skills. You can also invoke skills manually as slash commands. With this context loaded, agents respond faster and stay aligned with the project because the answer is either already in the context or the agent knows where to look. Note We do not endorse generating reference architecture content from scratch. The topic, main ideas, tradeoffs, and structure are expected to come from you, the contributing expert.
documents.s: Contributing to the Architecture Center with AI Agents

documents.t: Think of AGENTS.md as a project README tailored for agents. Many AI agents look for this file by default and load its content into the starting context on every new session. Other context files in the repository such as CLAUDE.md symlink to AGENTS.md, and .claude/skills symlinks to .agents/skills. This makes AGENTS.md and .agents/skills the single source of truth. If you want to propose changes to the project context, edit AGENTS.md. For skills, work in the .agents/skills folder. If you are working with Claude Code and want to override the project instructions with your own custom instructions, create a CLAUDE.local.md file in the repository root. Claude Code reads it automatically but it is git-ignored, so your personal overrides stay local.

Here are some things you can do today with the existing agent skills to get started. Ask the agent basic questions to familiarize yourself with the project: I just cloned the repository. What can I do with it? I saw something about reference architectures. Explain their purpose and the value they add. What are the concrete steps to make a contribution? Once you are ready to contribute, let the agent handle the formalities: I have new content on X in mind. Help me create the files for the new reference architecture. I want to see what the site looks like with my changes. Show me the rendered version. My contribution is ready for review. Go through the contribution process and create the PR. Best practice For creating new reference architectures, Quick Start remains the recommended path since it is purpose-built for that workflow.
